items.title: How I Turned QR-Coded Chips Into a Multi-Track Musical Instrument on iOS Without Core ML
items.author: Vitaliy Gribko
items.content:
My phone is lying face-up on a flat board. The board has a small transparent window cut into it. I slide a plastic chip underneath the window. A drum loop starts playing. I slide another chip in. A bass line joins. I pull one out and the drum track fades away over the next second.

That is the whole idea. Physical objects on a table become tracks in a mixer. No buttons, no touchscreen, no MIDI controller. Just chips with QR codes and a phone looking at them through a hole.

Each chip is a regular QR code containing a two-digit number,  through . That number maps to a track in a 24-channel audio mixer running inside the app. The camera scans the chips, the app fades the corresponding loops in and out. No Core ML. No neural network. The entire recognition pipeline is a single AVFoundation class that has been in iOS for years.

I started building this in September 2021. The first version had the camera, QR scanning, the audio engine, and the fade. It worked. I used it as a toy for a while. About a year and a half later, in March 2023, I returned to it. I added voice control, sample persistence, per-track volume, and packaged it as an MVP. The code has been sitting on my machine since. I recently decided that is a waste. If nothing else, the technical decisions are worth sharing. What started as a toy has since grown into an early-stage venture in music education. More on that at the end.

I listen to a lot of electronic music while working, Armin van Buuren's A State of Trance most weeks. So the idea of a board where you layer loops into a living mix was not a stretch for me. The app is not a tribute to any DJ. It is just what happens when an engineer who lives on weekly trance radio sits down to build a music toy.

This is a retrospective. The code is exactly as I left it in April 2023, rough edges and all.

The physical setup, a phone lying face-up on a flat board with a transparent window:

The app in action, detected chips appearing as on-screen cards with instrument icons over the live camera feed:

The app uses the front-facing camera. But that was not the original plan. For the entire first year and a half of development, from September 2021 through the MVP release in April 2023, the app used the rear camera. The switch to front happened in the last commit before I shelved the project. One line changed:  to .

The phone is lying face-up on the board. The screen faces the ceiling, showing you the camera feed and the chip overlays. With the rear camera pointing down through the cutout, the preview on screen is mirrored relative to your perspective. You move a chip left, the on-screen card moves right. The front camera solves this. The orientation matches your viewpoint. When you move a chip left, the card moves left.

It took me a year and a half to realize this was obvious. The rear camera worked for testing because I was holding the phone in my hand, pointing it at chips on a desk. The board with the cutout came later. Once I built the physical board and started using the app the way it was meant to be used, the orientation problem was immediately obvious. Two days after the MVP release, I switched the camera.

Before QR codes, there was Core ML. The first prototype did not use QR codes at all. Each chip had a printed image of an instrument on it. A drum kit, a guitar, a keyboard, a microphone. The app used a custom Core ML model to recognize which chip was in front of the camera.

I trained the model in Create ML, the tool that ships with Xcode. For each of the 24 chips, I took about 20 photos in different lighting, different backgrounds, different angles. 480 images total. Shooting them took a full day. You hold a chip, photograph it, turn it slightly, photograph again, move to a different table, photograph again, go outside, photograph again. Twenty times per chip, twenty-four chips. By the end of that day I never wanted to see those chips again.

Then the training. Create ML ran on my 2019 Intel MacBook with 16 GB of RAM. The model trained for 8 to 10 hours. I left it running overnight. More than one night, actually, because the first run always reveals something wrong with the dataset and you retake photos and retrain.

The result was decent. In daylight, recognition was around 90 to 95 percent, not bad for a first attempt. I thought about improving it: a hundred photos per chip instead of twenty would probably push accuracy higher, but a hundred photos per chip across 24 chips is 2,400 photos. That is not a weekend project. That is a data collection campaign.

There was also a more basic problem. The chips were physically identical. Same size, same material, same shape. The only difference was the printed instrument label, and those labels were small. The model was trying to distinguish between 24 objects that looked almost the same to a camera. I suspect the 5 to 10 percent error rate was mostly the model squinting at tiny details on identical chips.

The real dealbreaker was simpler: the model did not work at all in the dark. Core ML image classification needs enough light to extract features from the image. In a dim room, the instrument labels on the chips were invisible to the camera, and the model had nothing to go on.

One of the ideas behind the board was that a DJ could use it in a nightclub. Nightclubs are dark. The whole concept fell apart.

QR codes do not care about lighting. They are black and white, high contrast, and designed to be readable by machines. They generate in seconds. Adding a new chip means generating one QR code and printing it. No photo collection, no training, no overnight runs. The algorithm I will describe next worked on an iPhone 11, not even the Pro version, in 2021. It ran without lag even in debug mode on an iPhone SE. That was the moment I stopped thinking about Core ML for this project.

One Rectangle Is Not Enough

 is the built-in QR scanner in AVFoundation. You give it a region of interest and it scans that region for codes. The catch is that in practice, with the full frame as the region of interest, I was only reliably getting one code per frame. Put three chips on the table and it would pick up whichever one happened to be sharpest.

To be clear, the limit is documented - exactly once, in a 2013 technical note, , that practically nobody has read. The API returns an array of metadata objects per frame. But in my testing, with chips spread across the table at different distances from the camera, detection was unreliable for more than one at a time.

My best guess is autofocus. The camera locks focus on one depth plane, and codes outside that plane are too blurry for the detector. The detector itself might also have an internal per-frame budget that favors the sharpest candidate. I never confirmed this. I just needed it to work.

The workaround is to rotate through multiple overlapping regions. I defined six rectangles that together cover the full frame, with overlaps so nothing falls in a gap:

The coordinates are in normalized space, zero to one. Each rectangle is 0.33 wide (one third of the frame) and full height. They overlap by 0.165, which is half of 0.33. The last rectangle is only 0.165 wide because it only needs to cover the remaining strip on the right edge. The overlap ensures that a chip straddling two regions is always inside at least one.

Sharp-eyed readers will notice the rectangles actually cover 0 to 0.99. There is a one-percent strip on the right edge that is never scanned. I did not do this on purpose. I noticed it while writing this article, three years after the fact. In practice no chip has ever lived in that strip, because the transparent window in the board is smaller than the camera's field of view. But if you build this yourself, make the last rectangle 0.175 wide.

A timer switches  to the next rectangle every 0.2 seconds. A full sweep takes 1.2 seconds:

Why 0.2 seconds? Faster switching means better coverage but more CPU load and more metadata callbacks. Slower switching means a chip might sit undetected for up to 1.2 seconds if it lands in a gap between sweeps. 0.2 seconds was the sweet spot for a phone lying on a table with chips being moved by hand.

Why twenty-four chips, then, and not some rounder number? The detector hands back at most four codes per region, no matter how many are inside it. Six regions times four codes is twenty-four. The ceiling was never a product decision. It is exactly what one full sweep can see.

The limit belongs to the scanner, not to the concept. The audio side has no such wall: AVAudioEngine mixes as many player and EQ nodes as the CPU can feed, and twenty-four simultaneous loops sit nowhere near that edge.

Apple's , one import away in the same SDK since iOS 11, returns one observation per barcode it detects, dozens in a single frame. In 2021 we did not trust its barcode detection enough to bet the board on it. The board was also meant to run on iPhone 5-era dinosaurs. In 2021 they did not feel like dinosaurs. Neither did the old iPads people keep for a decade, and both kinds sat on the wrong side of Apple's 32-bit cutoff, below iOS 11, where Vision begins. The ceiling is a snapshot of that year's tools, not a law of nature. The board stayed at twenty-four because its detector was AVFoundation's , not because the number was magic.

The rectangles hid one more subtlety, and it cost me an evening.  is specified in metadata output coordinates, which are rotated relative to the video buffer. The origin is top-left and the coordinate system is landscape, even when the phone is in portrait. The rectangles look wrong if you think in screen coordinates. Apple documents this, but the documentation is one of those things you only understand after you have been bitten by it.

The whole scheme fits in one picture. Six rectangles a third of a frame wide, stepping across the view with half-width overlaps, while a timer walks them left to right and wraps. The red sliver on the right edge is the one percent nobody scans. The right panel holds both clocks: 1.2 seconds to sweep the whole table, and a 2.5 second window before a missing chip is considered gone.

The rotating scan, drawn to scale from the shipped searchRects. Five rectangles 0.33 wide and one 0.165, full frame height, each overlapping the next by half a rectangle so a straddling chip stays inside at least one. The timer advances rectOfInterest every 0.2 seconds; the whole table takes 1.2. The hatched sliver at the right edge is the one percent never scanned, and its fix is a single number: 0.175. Right panel: both timers, and the 2.5 second alive window that decides when a chip is really gone.

There is a problem with the rotating-rectangle approach. A chip might not be in the active scan region at the exact moment you check. So you cannot just start and stop tracks based on individual scan results. If a hand briefly covers a chip, or the sweep is on the other side of the frame, you do not want the music to cut out.

The solution is a time window. Every time a chip is detected, I store its bounds and a timestamp:

The metadata callback only writes to this dictionary. It does not touch the audio engine. A separate timer fires every 0.1 seconds, reads the dictionary, and makes all the play and stop decisions:

This is the most important UX decision in the whole app. Chip presence is time-windowed, not edge-triggered. A brief occlusion does not kill the track. The music keeps going for 2.5 seconds even if the scanner has not seen the chip again. That is long enough to survive a full sweep cycle with margin. The user never hears a glitch.

Why 2.5 seconds? The full sweep takes 1.2 seconds. A chip could be in a gap between two sweeps for up to 1.2 seconds. Add some margin for hand occlusion and camera latency. You pull a chip away, wait two and a half seconds, and then the fade-out begins. It feels intentional, like the music is giving the chip a chance to come back.

The thread separation matters too. The metadata callback runs on whatever queue AVFoundation decides. The audio engine should only be touched from one place. By splitting detection (write to dictionary) from audio control (read from dictionary on a timer), the audio engine is never touched from the camera callback thread. All audio control happens on a predictable 0.1-second cadence.

 is Apple's graph-based audio framework. Each track in the mixer is two nodes: a player node that produces audio from a file, and an EQ node that controls volume. The app supports 24 tracks, but only creates tracks that have a WAV file assigned to them. This keeps the engine light when you are using three chips instead of twenty-four:

I am not doing any actual equalization. The EQ node is used purely as a volume control through its  parameter. It just happens to be the cheapest way to get a gain stage in the AVAudioEngine graph. The mixer node combines all tracks into a single output.

The keys are zero-padded two-digit strings:  through . This matters because the QR codes on the chips contain exactly these strings. When the scanner reads , that string goes directly to loopPlayer.turnOn(index: "07"), which looks up . The zero-padding is not cosmetic. It is the contract between the physical world and the audio engine. A chip with  instead of  would not match anything.

The audio session is configured for  with output forced to the built-in speaker. The phone is lying face-up. You want the sound coming out of the bottom speaker, not routed to a connected AirPod that happens to be sitting in your pocket. But this creates a problem I will get to when I talk about voice control.

Making a WAV file loop without a gap between repetitions is a classic AVFoundation problem.  with  does not work inside . You have to schedule segments manually.

The trick is to schedule the next playback segment inside the completion handler of the current one. Each segment starts at the sample position where the previous one ends. A simple boolean flag controls whether the loop continues:

 is a class with a boolean inside it. I needed reference semantics so the completion handler can read the current value. When , the next time the handler fires it will not schedule another segment. The loop stops gracefully at the end of the current iteration.

The handler calls itself recursively, scheduling the file at the next sample position each time.  accumulates the total offset, so each segment is scheduled at the exact sample position where the previous one ends.  pre-buffers the first segment so playback starts immediately. This is a standard pattern. Apple's documentation covers it, though not in one place. You piece it together from the AVAudioPlayerNode reference and various WWDC sessions.

When a chip appears or disappears, the track fades in or out over one second. Hard cuts sound terrible. A drum loop that suddenly drops to zero feels like a mistake. A one-second fade feels like a musical transition.

Here is where I will be honest about a hack. The fade is implemented as a loop that steps the volume up or down by one percent at a time, with a  between each step:

Each step sleeps for  seconds. The  adjusts for partial fades. If a track is already at 60 percent and fading to 100, the fade takes 0.4 seconds instead of a full second. That matches how our ears work.

The fade runs on a global dispatch queue and is cancellable.  and  store the current  for each track. If a chip reappears while its track is fading out, the fade-out is cancelled and the fade-in starts from the current volume. That part works well.

There is a bonus oddity at the end of the work item: it cancels whatever is stored in  for its own index, which at that point is itself. Cancelling a  that is already running does nothing, so this is harmless. It is a leftover from an earlier version where the bookkeeping was done differently. I left it in the code sample because that is what the code actually looks like. Every codebase has a line like this.

The part that does not work well is the . Blocking a GCD thread is not something you should do in production code. It introduces jitter because the sleep is not precise. On a busy device the steps can bunch up or stretch out. For a prototype with one-second fades on five tracks, you do not hear it. But if I were building this for real, I would use  parameter automation or a render-callback ramp. Those are sample-accurate and do not block any threads. At minimum, a -driven timer would be better than .

Every prototype has parts like this. Nobody expects prototype code to be perfect. What matters is whether the idea behind it is worth pursuing.

The tap handler for a chip's card has the same problem. It takes the layer's name and force-unwraps it as an integer:

If the layer name is ever not a number, the app crashes. In practice the layer names are always the QR code values, which are always two-digit numbers, so it has never crashed in testing. But that is not a safety guarantee. That is luck. A guard let index = Int(title) else { return } would be the correct version. I knew this when I wrote it. I left it because the prototype worked and I moved on to the next feature. That is how technical debt accumulates in a solo project with no deadlines.

There is also the overlay rendering. Every 0.1 seconds,  throws away all sublayers and rebuilds them from scratch. detectionOverlay.sublayers = nil, then re-add everything. For five or six chips, this is fine. But it does not scale. If you wanted twenty-four chips with complex overlays, you would want to diff and update existing layers instead of nuking everything ten times a second.

A detected chip appears on screen as a rounded rectangle with an instrument icon and a track number. The rectangle is drawn at the position where the QR code was found in the camera frame. This sounds simple, but coordinate conversion between the camera buffer and the screen is fiddly.

The metadata output gives you normalized bounds (zero to one). You multiply by  to get buffer-space coordinates. Then you need to transform from buffer space to view space, accounting for the fact that the camera is rotated 90 degrees relative to the screen:

The CGAffineTransform(rotationAngle: .pi / 2.0).scaledBy(x: 1.0, y: -1.0) does two things. It rotates the layer 90 degrees to match the screen orientation. It also flips the layer vertically, undoing the mirroring from the front camera and the buffer-to-view conversion. Without this transform, the chip cards would appear sideways and mirrored. I arrived at this particular combination of rotation and scale empirically, one build at a time. That is how most camera-to-screen transform code gets written.

The instrument icon is determined by the track number. Tracks 1 through 6 show a vocal icon, 7 through 12 a drum icon, 13 through 18 a guitar icon, and 19 and above a keyboard icon. These are just visual groupings. There is no audio difference between a track in the vocal range and one in the drum range. But the icons help you find what you are looking for when you have six chips on the table.

Human hearing is logarithmic. A linear volume slider feels wrong. The app converts the 0 to 100 percent slider value to decibels before setting the EQ gain:

At 100 percent the gain is 0 dB. At 10 percent it is about -48 dB. At 1 percent the formula gives -96 dB, which is the minimum clamp and effectively silence. The inverse function converts back from dB to percent for the slider position. This is not exotic audio engineering. It is the kind of thing every audio app should do and many do not.

Volume and track assignments are persisted in . Each track stores a  struct with the WAV filename and its keyword string. On launch,  reads them back and knows which WAV to load for each track. For 24 tracks with one integer and one struct each,  is perfectly adequate. No reason to reach for Core Data or SQLite.

Assigning a loop to a track is done by voice. You long-press a sample in the list. The app starts listening through . You say something like "fast drums with afro rhythm." The speech recognizer returns the text. The app splits it into words and matches them against a keyword dictionary:

Each sample slot has a list of keywords. Track 06 has ["drums", "fast", "afro", "house", "lounge"]. Track 24 has ["fast", "speed", "paced", "high", "frequency", "house", "techno", "danceable", "drums", "kick"]. The matcher counts how many of the spoken words appear in each track's keyword list. The track with the most matches wins. If nothing matches, it picks a random track.

If you look closely at the function name, that  in  is not a Latin C. It is Cyrillic. I switched keyboard layouts while typing and did not notice. Swift does not care, and it compiles fine. It shipped to the repo like that, and I only spotted it years later when reviewing the code for this article. That is the kind of thing that happens when you are the only developer and there is no code review.

This is a crude approach. No embeddings, no semantic similarity, no NLP. But it works well enough for the prototype. For a kids' education product, this is the kind of interaction that feels magical. A child says "fast drums" and a drum loop appears on the track they are holding.

The speech recognizer manages its own  instance for microphone input. It installs a tap on bus 0, captures audio in 1024-sample chunks, and streams them to the recognition request:

Now for the problem I mentioned earlier. The audio session is set to  for the mixer. When voice control activates, it switches to . On iOS, you cannot have both at the same time with these categories. Switching to  interrupts the playback engine. The music stops while you are assigning a sample. You long-press a sample, the music cuts out, you speak, the music comes back when the session returns to .

You can use  to allow simultaneous playback and recording. But that category has its own quirks, including audio routing changes that can send playback to the receiver instead of the speaker. For the prototype, I accepted the interruption. You do not assign samples often. When you do, a brief silence is acceptable. For a production app, I would use  with careful output port management, or pre-record the assignments in a separate session.

Imagine the same setup but for learning. A child has a board with a transparent window. Underneath the window they slide chips. Instead of drum loops, each chip plays a spoken number. Slide the chip with  and the app says "seven." Slide it next to the chip with  and the app says "seven, three." Arrange them in sequence and the child is composing numbers while learning to count.

The beats I use in my own demo are licensed audio, and I cannot redistribute them. So the repo ships with 24 WAV files instead, each one a spoken number from one to twenty-four. They demonstrate the audio pipeline without any licensing issues. You replace them with your own loops and the app works the same way.

The same mechanic scales to other educational content. Letters. Animal sounds. Colors in different languages. The QR code is just an identifier. The audio file is just a resource. The board and chips are just the physical interface.

There is also a second road I keep thinking about, and 2026 made it realistic. Earlier in this article I described dropping Core ML because training a recognizer was a data collection campaign. Generation is the opposite trade. The chips stay what they are, simple QR identifiers. But instead of shipping recorded loops, the model would generate the audio for each chip on the fly from a text description. This chip becomes a drum beat in a chosen style. That one becomes a bass line at a set tempo. A third speaks a phrase in another language. The user still arranges and mixes entirely with chips, exactly the way they do today. Every chip carries its own generated sound; the composition is entirely yours.

Voice assignment gets the same upgrade. Today the app matches spoken words against hand-written keyword lists, and the matcher simply counts hits. A model that understands the phrase would replace the whole dictionary: you say what the chip should be, in any wording, and the generated audio matches it. The heavy lifting moves into the model, and the physical interface stays light.

The detector gets an upgrade too. Vision, the framework this article left on the table in 2021, has no four-per-region habit and no rotated coordinate space. Swap AVCaptureMetadataOutput for it, and the ceiling dissolves. Twenty-four stops being a limit and becomes a design choice.

The number was not the only limit. A board full of loops is still one person's taste. That is fixable too. Someone assembles a drum kit in Austin, someone else loads it in Ibiza the same evening, and the board stops belonging to one table. The chips stay dumb numbers, the QR codes stay on paper, and what travels is the sound packs behind them. The packs themselves would travel over the internet, through the platform's own backend, and no chip would ever change hands. A library like that turns twenty-four slots into twenty-four doors, and it needs no new hardware.

Words travel the same channel. A teacher in one city drops this week's vocabulary onto a board, and a child in another plays the words off the chips that evening. That makes the board a mailbox too.

Whichever of those roads it takes, the idea has already grown beyond a solo side project into an early-stage venture. A physical product needs a board, a set of chips, and a phone app that turns the whole thing into an interactive learning tool for children. The prototype works, and the concept holds up. Getting from there to a real product takes skills I do not have alone. That is a job for a team, not for one developer in the evenings.

The full source is on GitHub. iOS, Swift, no third-party dependencies. Just AVFoundation and UIKit.

The whole prototype, in numbers:

  •  tracks, each two nodes: a player and a gain stage.
  •  scan rectangles;  per step,  per full sweep.
  •  alive window before a chip counts as gone.
  •  training photos and  of Create ML, replaced by  printable QR codes.
  •  line of code to move the camera to the front.
  •  timers:  for audio decisions,  for the sweep.
  •  third-party dependencies.
  • A year and a half from toy to MVP, and three and a half more years to this retrospective.

Clone it, open it in Xcode, run it on a real iPhone (the simulator does not have a camera). Print a few QR codes with two-digit numbers. Put them on chips or cards. Point the phone at them and the loops start playing.

If you work in education, hardware, or just find this idea interesting, I would be glad to hear from you. The prototype is the proof that the concept works. Taking it further needs hardware design, educational content, and people who know how to bring a physical product to market.

The code is MIT licensed. The concept and design are mine. Build it, try it, and let me know what you think.

items.title: Where Satellite Positioning Fails: Fighting Bluetooth RSSI Chaos With Levenberg-Marquardt
items.author: Vitaliy Gribko
items.content:
Satellite positioning gets you to the building. Inside the building, it abandons you. The signals that triangulate your position to within a few meters outdoors cannot penetrate a roof. Concrete and steel kill the signal. Inside a warehouse, a hospital, a shopping mall, an airport terminal, you are invisible to every satellite constellation humanity has launched.

This is the indoor positioning problem, and it is genuinely hard. Not hard in the "interesting engineering puzzle" sense. Hard in the "the laws of physics are working against you" sense. I built an iOS app called BeaconIL that attempts to solve it using Bluetooth Low Energy beacons and a non-linear optimization algorithm ported from numerical computing. This is the story of what I learned fighting radio physics with math.

A bit of context on why this project exists. By 2020 I had spent twelve years in total across desktop development and embedded work on microcontrollers, moving from Qt and C++ on desktop down to bare-metal firmware. I worked in the R&D department of a company that built microcontroller-based products. No two assignments were alike. Firmware for hazardous-gas monitoring in the metro. Industrial infrastructure monitoring. And  that later scaled to a nationwide launch, a journey I have written about already. Then came the assignment that matters to this story: smartwatches destined for factory production, with indoor positioning on the feature list, because satellite fixes die under a roof. There was a safety angle too. A factory floor has machinery that does not forgive a half-meter mistake, so the position had to be trustworthy up close, not merely accurate on average.

The watch was the main deliverable. To give it something to range against, we built our own iBeacons as well: one colleague designed the hardware, and the firmware was my part. The heart of the assignment, though, was the math: turning noisy radio readings into a position estimate on a microcontroller, eventually in plain C. But hunting down the radio pitfalls was easiest with a phone in hand. iOS handed me a working BLE stack, ranging callbacks out of CoreLocation, and a screen to plot the estimate on. None of it needed debugging; it arrived working. On the microcontroller, those layers would have been mine to build before the math could even be tested. So the algorithm first went to iOS and became BeaconIL. Once the algorithm proved itself on real hardware, I ported it to Go as a clean standalone library. That Go code was meant as the reference for the final C rewrite on the microcontroller, this time without the bugs I had already found. So at the time BeaconIL started, none of that math existed yet. The destination was a bare-metal microcontroller, but the phone let me focus on the math alone. It brought its own OS abstraction layer and its own constraints, of course. The experiment answered more than it was asked. Working so closely on iOS, by the way, settled my direction. After this project I chose mobile as the career to build, the apps I shipped there got noticed, and my manager eventually asked for a corporate one as well.

The primary goal wasn't to build a polished product. It was to validate the math, to prove that EMA filtering, the path-loss distance model, and Levenberg-Marquardt trilateration would produce a stable, usable position estimate on real iOS hardware with real BLE beacons. That goal was met. In a 4 by 6 meter room with three calibrated beacons, the on-screen marker stayed within about half a meter of where I actually stood. Shipping on the App Store, passing two review cycles, and eventually open-sourcing it were all secondary. If I rebuilt this today with the mobile experience I've since accumulated, the architecture would look different: cleaner, more idiomatic to iOS, less like an embedded engineer's first mobile project. But raw architecture is not unreliable code. Those early apps held up in real use, and the corner cases that mattered were handled. The math, which was the point, works.

The app scans for iBeacon-compatible BLE beacons in the vicinity, measures the signal strength of each one, converts that to a distance estimate, and then runs a trilateration algorithm to compute a position. It renders the result in real time on a floor plan. It went through two App Store review cycles and shipped. The code is at https://github.com/Vitaliy69/BeaconIL.

Bluetooth Low Energy beacons are small, battery-powered transmitters that broadcast advertising packets at regular intervals, typically 10 times per second. Each packet contains a UUID, a major value, and a minor value, identifying the beacon and its group. The iPhone picks these packets up via CoreLocation. CoreLocation batches them and delivers a single  callback about once per second, containing an array of all visible beacons with their current RSSI values. RSSI is measured in decibel-milliwatts (dBm).

RSSI is a negative number. The closer to zero, the stronger the signal. A beacon right next to your phone might read -40 dBm. Walk ten meters away and you might see -75 dBm. In theory, this gives you a way to estimate distance: weaker signal means farther away.

In practice, RSSI is one of the noisiest signals you will ever work with. The radio wave that leaves the beacon does not travel in a clean straight line to your phone. It bounces off walls, floors, ceilings, metal shelves, and human bodies. It gets absorbed by water (and humans are mostly water). It interferes with itself through multipath propagation: the same packet arrives via multiple paths at slightly different times, and the copies add up or cancel each other out. A person walking between you and the beacon can drop the RSSI by 10 dBm in an instant, then it snaps back when they pass.

Standing perfectly still, holding the phone perfectly steady, the RSSI from a single beacon will jitter by 3 to 8 dBm from one reading to the next. Since the RSSI-to-distance conversion is logarithmic, a 6 dBm jitter at 3 meters translates to a distance swing of roughly −1.5 to +3 meters. The asymmetry comes from the logarithmic curve. Your position estimate would be bouncing around like a pinball.

This is the first wall you hit. You have to deal with it before any positioning math is even possible.

EMA: Exponential Moving Average

The solution is signal filtering. You cannot use the raw RSSI values. They're too volatile. You need to smooth them. But you cannot smooth too aggressively, or the system becomes sluggish and the position lags behind actual movement.

I chose an Exponential Moving Average, or EMA. The idea is simple: each new RSSI reading nudges the smoothed value by a small fraction, rather than replacing it entirely. The fraction is controlled by a smoothing coefficient derived from a window size :

α = 2 / (N + 1)
ema_new = α × rssi_new + (1 - α) × ema_old

The implementation in  maintains a per-beacon RSSI history buffer. When a new reading arrives, it checks whether the buffer has filled past the EMA window size. If not, it simply appends the raw value, since there is not enough data to smooth yet. Once the buffer is full, the EMA formula kicks in:

The window slides: old values drop off the front as new ones come in. The default window size is 10, which gives a smoothing coefficient of about 0.18. That means each new reading contributes roughly 18% to the smoothed value, and the remaining 82% is carried forward from history.

The window size is user-configurable, ranging from 5 to 100. A smaller window makes the system more responsive (the position updates quickly when you move) but lets more noise through. A larger window is smoother but lags. I settled on 10 as the default after testing with actual beacons in a real room. It was the sweet spot where the position marker on screen moved deliberately rather than jittering, but did not feel like it was swimming through molasses.

There is also a staleness check. If a beacon has not been heard from in 12 seconds, it is evicted from the buffer entirely. This handles the case where you walk out of range of a beacon. You do not want stale data from a beacon you can no longer see polluting the trilateration.

Once you have a smoothed RSSI value, you need to convert it to a distance. The model used is a simplified version of the log-distance path loss equation:

distance = 10 ^ ((txCalibratedPower - rssi) / (10 × n))

Here,  is the RSSI measured at exactly 1 meter from the beacon. It is the reference point, the anchor that ties the abstract dBm numbers to physical distance. The  is the path-loss exponent: in free space, signal power decays with the square of distance, and n = 2 accounts for the 20·log₁₀(d) term in the Friis transmission equation. That free-space 2 is the value the app shipped with. Real buildings rarely agree with it, which is what the calibration recipe later in this article is about. The frequency is baked into the 1-meter reference value, not into the exponent.

The implementation is a single function:

That divisor in the code, , is the same 10 × n from the formula above. The exponent became a parameter , with the default preserving the original 2021 behavior for both existing call sites. When you scale the calibration recipe below to a real floor,  is the number you fit per zone.

If  is -59 dBm, typical for an Estimote or Kontakt.io beacon, and your smoothed RSSI reads -70 dBm, the distance works out to about 10^(11/20) ≈ 3.5 meters with the free-space default. Fit the same reading against a site exponent of 2.8 and the estimate shrinks to 10^(11/28) ≈ 2.5 meters. Same radio, same arithmetic, a meter of difference bought entirely by the exponent. Simple enough.

But  is not a universal constant. Every beacon is slightly different. Manufacturing tolerances, antenna orientation, battery level, enclosure material: all of it shifts the 1-meter reference by a few dBm. If you assume -59 for a beacon whose true value is -65, your distance estimates will be systematically off by a factor of 10^(6/20) ≈ 2x. You would think a beacon 2 meters away is 4 meters away. The entire system would be broken.

This is why calibration exists.

BeaconIL includes a calibration mode. You place your iPhone exactly 1 meter from a beacon, at the same height, and press "Start calibration." The app then collects RSSI measurements (30 by default) and averages them to produce the  for that specific beacon.

The live RSSI value is displayed during calibration so you can watch it stabilize. Once enough samples are collected, the average is stored as that beacon's  in Core Data. The calibration data size is configurable: you can collect anywhere from 10 to 150 samples. More samples means a better average but a longer calibration session. Thirty was a practical default: it takes about 30 seconds at CoreLocation's roughly one-callback-per-second delivery rate and produces a stable enough reference. The full round trip through the app, notifications and all, shows up later in this article.

The app warns you not to background it during calibration, because iOS suspends BLE ranging when the app is not foregrounded. You would get stale or missing readings and the calibration would be garbage.

One more honest caveat. The exponent of 2 in the distance formula is the free-space value, and real buildings are not free space. Measured indoor exponents run from about 1.6 in open halls to 4 and higher behind concrete. Calibration anchors the curve at 1 meter, so estimates stay honest at short range. With the exponent fixed at 2, the far end of the curve drifts systematically. In a 4 by 6 meter room that drift is tolerable. In a warehouse it would not be.

Scaling the calibration to a real floor is its own procedure, and the room-versus-factory gap is exactly where it starts. A practical recipe:

Walk the site first, before mounting anything. Note metal racks, freezer aisles, moving machinery, people flows. These decide your exponent neighborhoods: published measurements put it near 2 in open space, 2.7 to 3.5 in offices, and 4 or higher in cluttered industrial halls. Your 4 by 6 meter lab numbers do not transfer.

Calibrate each beacon at 1 meter where it will live, not where it is convenient. Then take reference measurements along a baseline: stand at known distances, 2, 4, 8 meters, and log RSSI. Two points per zone are enough to fit a local exponent: fit the line through measured pairs on a log-distance plot, and the slope is your n. Feed that n back into  for beacons in that zone; it is exactly the  parameter from the listing above. A zone behind a concrete wall deserves its own exponent and should not share one with open floor.

Recalibrate on a schedule. Racks move, inventory turns over, layouts change. Published deployment guides suggest quarterly recalibration for high-accuracy applications. And when the environment refuses to behave, drop the physics model entirely. The alternative is fingerprinting: you record RSSI patterns at known reference points, then match live readings against that map. It trades the model for measured reality and is the standard answer for large irregular spaces.

Why Linear Trilateration Fails

That was calibration at deployment scale. Back inside one room, with one phone: you have distances to at least three beacons, and you know where each beacon sits on the floor plan. Time to find your position.

The textbook approach is trilateration: draw a circle around each beacon with radius equal to the measured distance. The point where all three circles intersect is your position. Clean, elegant, and in the real world, completely broken.

The problem is that your distance estimates are never exact. They are approximations derived from noisy radio signals that have been filtered but not purified. So in practice, the three circles almost never intersect at a single point. They overlap in a messy region, or they do not overlap at all. Two circles might intersect at two points, the third might miss both. There is no clean geometric solution.

You could try averaging the intersection points, or taking the centroid of the overlap region. These hacks work poorly. They ignore that some distance estimates are more reliable than others. A nearby beacon with a strong signal gives a better estimate than a distant one at the noise floor.

The correct approach is to stop treating this as a geometry problem and start treating it as an optimization problem: find the best position given imperfect distance measurements.

Levenberg-Marquardt: Non-Linear Least Squares

Instead of looking for a perfect intersection, you define a cost function that measures how bad any candidate position is, and then you minimize it. The cost function is the sum of squared residuals, formulated as the difference of squared distances:

f(x) = Σ ( ‖x - pᵢ‖² - dᵢ² )²

Where  is the candidate position,  is the known position of beacon , and  is the measured distance to that beacon. For each beacon, you compute the squared Euclidean distance from your candidate position to the beacon, subtract the squared measured distance, square the difference, and sum over all beacons. The position that minimizes this sum is your best estimate. This formulation (difference of squares rather than difference of distances) shares its minimizer with the direct form whenever an exact solution exists; on noisy data the two can differ slightly. In exchange, the squared form produces a simpler Jacobian. The partial derivatives become linear in the coordinates (), so each LMA iteration is cheaper to compute.

This is a non-linear least squares problem, and the standard tool for solving it is the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. LMA is a hybrid between gradient descent and the Gauss-Newton method, and it adapts its behavior based on how close it is to the solution. Far from the minimum it behaves like gradient descent: slow but reliable, taking small steps in the direction of steepest descent. Close to the minimum it switches to Gauss-Newton: fast convergence, with larger, more precise steps. The switch is controlled by a damping parameter λ that gets adjusted at each iteration based on whether the step reduced the cost.

The full implementation is in : 771 lines of Swift with no external dependencies. It is a port of the Apache Commons Math Levenberg-Marquardt optimizer, originally written in Java. The same algorithm also lives in an open-source Go library, . Its initial commit is dated June 28, 2021, the same day the Swift core received its hardening update with additional checks and 3D space support. Two independent implementations of the same math, validating each other ever since.

While preparing this article, I checked the two ports against each other on shared test vectors. On inputs that admit an exact solution, both return the same coordinates to twelve decimal places. On noisy inputs the results agree to within a micrometer, and the small remainder is floating-point rounding, not a difference in logic

The cover image of this article is built the same way. Three beacons sit on it at fixed coordinates. The circles are measured distances, derived from realistic RSSI values through the path-loss formula. That red star is not decoration. It is the solver's answer for that exact scene, computed while the cover was being drawn. The true position I seeded the scene with sits a few centimeters away, because the noisy circles pull the estimate off the geometric ideal. That drift is the whole story of this article in one picture. If you run those three circles through either port, you land within a hair of the same point.

Both ports have test suites that run from a single command. The Swift package builds the solver with a test executable; the Go module has . They share the same vectors: exact inputs, noisy inputs, higher-dimensional anchors, and malformed inputs that must be rejected. On the rejection side the two implementations earned their guards differently. Swift got its dimensionality check in the June 2021 commit. Go caught up only years later, when its own test suite panicked on mixed-dimension anchors, the same bug the Swift version had fixed two years earlier. The fix landed in the repository the same day the panic surfaced. A port is not done until it fails the same way as the original.

One run of the Go library compresses the whole story into a single scene. Feed it four anchors and four noisy distances, and it starts at the centroid, feels which way the cost function slopes, and takes carefully damped steps until the estimate stops moving. The scene below is that exact run, traced from the solver's own loop. Each translucent sphere is one noisy distance. The red path is the estimate walking downhill. The star is where it settled, about half a meter from the truth. The panels on the right show the same run from the inside: the cost collapsing, and the damping rising once to brake a bad step. When damping reaches zero, the solver is taking pure Gauss-Newton steps.

The Swift entry point is solve(positions:distances:):

That comment has the signs wrong.  is always zero. The actual equation at the optimum is (x0-xi)^2 + (y0-yi)^2 - ri^2 = target[i], matching the cost function above, but the comment reads  and  instead. It is harmless. Comments do not execute. The  and  functions below compute the correct thing. Call it a small blemish that survived in the shipped code.

A few design decisions are worth spelling out.

 The optimizer needs a starting guess. I use the centroid, the average of all beacon positions. This is a reasonable starting point because the device is somewhere in the area covered by the beacons, and the centroid is in the middle of that area. A better initial guess means fewer iterations to converge.

Inverse square weighting. Each beacon's contribution to the cost function is weighted by . This means closer beacons (which have more reliable distance estimates) have more influence on the solution. A beacon at 1 meter has 25 times more weight than one at 5 meters. This is the inverse square law, and it mirrors the physical reality that signal strength degrades with the square of distance: measurements made closer to the source are inherently more trustworthy.

 The optimizer stops when the relative reduction in cost falls below 1e-10, or when the step size becomes smaller than 1e-10 times the parameter norm. These are tight tolerances, so the algorithm does not stop early. It also has hard limits of 1000 iterations and 1000 function evaluations as a safety net, though in practice it converges in 5 to 20 iterations.

 At each iteration, the Jacobian matrix (the matrix of partial derivatives of the residuals with respect to the position parameters) is decomposed using QR factorization with column pivoting. This is numerically stable and handles rank-deficient cases gracefully. The implementation includes a full QR decomposition routine with Householder reflections, column pivoting for numerical stability, and Givens rotations for the LM parameter determination.

The Jacobian for this problem is straightforward. The partial derivative of the residual with respect to each coordinate is simply :

The residual function computes the squared distance difference:

Put it all together and you get a position estimate that's robust to noisy distances. Instead of demanding that three circles meet at a point (which they never will in practice), the algorithm finds the position that best fits the available data, weighted by how trustworthy each measurement is. When a fourth or fifth beacon is visible, the system automatically uses all of them. More beacons means more constraints, which means a better fit. The algorithm does not care about the geometry of "three circles". It just minimizes error.

Thread Isolation: Keeping the UI Alive

BLE scanning produces a steady stream of updates. CoreLocation delivers one  callback per second, and each callback contains an array of all visible beacons with fresh RSSI values. With 5 beacons visible, that is 5 updated  objects arriving every second. That is not a huge load, but if you process it carelessly on the main thread, the UI can still suffer. The table view will stutter, the SpriteKit scene will drop frames, and the app will feel broken.

The solution is explicit thread management.  processes the ranging callback (filtering known beacons, computing distances, building the diffable data source snapshot) and then explicitly hops to the main thread to apply the snapshot and trigger the visualization update:

The notification triggers  in , which runs IndoorMath.updateVisibleBeacons() and . These are pure computation (EMA filtering, distance conversion, and the LMA solver), and they run on the main thread because the result is immediately consumed by the SpriteKit scene. For an MVP that is a deliberate trade. The solver converges in microseconds for three to five beacons, so a background queue would only add context-switching overhead without any visible benefit. I measured it. An optimized build of , run in a loop over two fixed scenes with three and five beacons, averaged about 5 microseconds per solve for three beacons and about 10 for five, on a current Mac desktop. A phone will be slower, but still in microseconds. By Geekbench single-core scores, an iPhone 11 runs at roughly 2.5x slower than this Mac, which lands a five-beacon solve in the tens of microseconds. The argument does not change.

The snapshot is fully built before anything touches the UI, and that's the part that matters.  then guarantees it's applied on the main thread, regardless of which queue delivered the ranging callback.  also holds a  flag that  sets to  in , so the scan controller stops processing entirely when the user is not looking at the scan screen. There is no point burning CPU on trilateration when nobody is watching.

SpriteKit as a Floor Plan Renderer

For the visualization layer, I used SpriteKit, Apple's 2D game engine. This might seem like an odd choice for a utility app. UIKit would have been more conventional. But SpriteKit gives you a scene graph with a coordinate system, z-ordering, and built-in animation, all of which are useful for rendering a floor plan with moving objects.

The  class manages the scene. Beacons are drawn as blue square sprites, the device position as a red marker. A floor-plan image can be loaded from the photo library and placed as a background layer at 50% opacity:

The  system ensures the background is always behind the beacons and the position marker. When the scene is updated, all existing beacon and location nodes are removed and re-added with fresh positions. This is not the most efficient approach (you could update existing nodes in place), but for a handful of objects it is fast enough and avoids the complexity of node pooling.

The scene's coordinate system is centered at (0, 0) and extends outward based on the "View Area Size" setting. Beacon coordinates are stored relative to this center point. If you set a beacon's X to 5.0 and Y to -3.0, it appears 5 units to the right and 3 units below center on the scene. The scale factor maps scene units to pixels, and it adjusts when the area size changes.

One nice detail: the  on the  is set to 1. This sounds wrong. Why would you want 1 fps on a game engine? But this is not a game. The scene does not need to render continuously at 60 fps. It only needs to redraw when there is new position data, which happens when a ranging callback arrives. Setting the frame rate to 1 means SpriteKit ticks the scene once per second, which is enough to keep the background and node positions fresh without burning battery on unnecessary renders. The actual position updates happen on-demand via , which directly manipulates the node tree.

Persistence: Core Data, Codable, and CloudKit

Beacon configurations (coordinates, calibrated RSSI, names) need to survive app restarts and sync across devices. The architecture here has three layers.

 is a plain  struct:

Each beacon's configuration is serialized to JSON and stored as a string in a Core Data entity called . The entity has a single attribute, , which holds the JSON string. A computed property  handles encoding and decoding transparently:

This is an unconventional pattern. Normally you would model each field as a separate Core Data attribute rather than stuffing JSON into a single string. But there is a practical reason for it: CloudKit. When Core Data syncs through CloudKit, every attribute becomes a separate field in the CloudKit schema, and schema changes require a migration. By storing the configuration as a single JSON string, the CloudKit schema stays simple and stable. Adding a new field to  is just a Codable change: no migration, no CloudKit schema update.

 is the CRUD layer. It fetches all beacons on init, provides  and  methods, and saves through the . The context has automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent enabled, so changes from CloudKit sync are reflected without manual merge logic.

 The  lazily initializes the persistent container. If iCloud sync is enabled (the default), it uses NSPersistentCloudKitContainer instead of a plain :

When CloudKit is enabled, Core Data automatically syncs changes to iCloud and across the user's devices. Configure beacons on your iPad, and they appear on your iPhone. The entitlements file declares the CloudKit container identifier and services. When sync is disabled, the app falls back to local-only storage with persistent history tracking enabled (which is required for proper change handling without CloudKit).

The Calibration Loop, End to End

Let me walk through what actually happens when you calibrate a beacon, because it touches nearly every component.

You tap a beacon in the list, which triggers a segue to . You see fields for X, Y, RSSI, and name. You enter the beacon's physical coordinates on your floor plan, say (5.0, 3.0), and a name like "B1". The RSSI field defaults to -59, a common factory value.

You press "Start calibration." An alert tells you to place the phone 1 meter from the beacon at the same height. You confirm. The  flag is set to true, the RSSI field is disabled, and a notification is posted:

 receives this notification and stores the beacon being calibrated. On the next ranging callback, it filters the visible beacons to find the one matching the major/minor values and posts its raw RSSI back:

 receives each RSSI value, increments the counter, and accumulates the sum. The live RSSI is displayed so you can see the readings coming in: -61, -58, -63, -60, -59... When the count reaches the configured calibration data size (default 30), the average is computed and stored:

The  on  fires, which posts the stop notification, displays the final value, re-enables the field, and resets the accumulators. You press Save, and  persists the calibrated beacon to Core Data. If CloudKit is on, it syncs to your other devices.

Now, when this beacon is visible during scanning,  uses the calibrated RSSI as  in the distance calculation. The 1-meter reference is no longer a guess. It is a measured value for this specific physical beacon, in this specific environment, with this specific phone.

The app isn't on the App Store anymore, but it did make it there. It shipped under the name "Beacon Indoor Location," App Store ID 1561643830, through two released versions, 1.0 and 1.2, both of which cleared Apple's review. Version 1.2 went all the way through App Store Review and came out the other side with the status "Ready for Distribution." The listing came down later, not over anything wrong with the app, but because the commercial developer account behind it was temporarily frozen. By then BeaconIL had already done what it set out to do. It proved the concept end to end, from a raw BLE signal to a dot on a floor plan, inside a real consumer iOS app that Apple approved. What's left is an architecture that could be scaled further and adapted to infrastructure standards for the US market, if that path is ever taken. The code lives on, open source under the MIT license.

The Math Evolved: A Bug and a Generalization

The git history tells its own story, and it shows how the math actually matured.

The first commit landed on April 22, 2021. The entire codebase, 3,947 lines across 71 files, went in as a single "First public commit." That is not unusual for a solo project that was developed privately and then pushed to a remote. What is unusual is what happened next: nothing, for two months. Then on June 28, a second commit touched only two files:  and . The commit message described the change as additional checks plus support for more than two dimensions.

That commit fixed a subtle but serious problem. In the original code, the iteration and evaluation counters were initialized to the maximum values themselves (1000 and 1000) instead of 0 and 1:

And there were no checks against these limits anywhere in the loop. The counters existed but were never enforced. If the optimizer failed to converge (say, because of pathological beacon geometry or wildly inconsistent distances), the  loop would spin forever, freezing the app. The limits looked like a safety net, but nothing ever enforced them.

The June update fixed both issues. The counters were properly initialized to 0 and 1, and actual limit checks were added inside the loop:

The  and  were also moved from instance variables to  constants, a minor Swift refactoring that makes them proper compile-time constants on the type rather than per-instance values.

The second change in that commit was the return type. The original  function returned a fixed 2D tuple:

The file header said "Solves a formulation of n-D space trilateration problem (2D in this application)." The updated version dropped the parenthetical and changed the return type to a generic array:

Now the solver returns a coordinate array matching whatever dimensionality the input positions have. The caller in  still unpacks only the first two elements because the app's floor plan is flat, but the solver itself is not limited to two axes. The Jacobian, the residual function, and the QR decomposition all operate on arbitrary dimensions, so the same code can handle multi-level retail store layouts without modification.

That commit also added a dimension-validation check: if the input positions have inconsistent dimensionality, the solver returns an empty array instead of producing garbage. The measurements get the same treatment: a zero, negative, or non-finite distance, or a non-finite anchor coordinate, is rejected up front. The reason is the weighting. Inverse square weighting turns a zero distance into an infinite weight, and one NaN travels through the QR decomposition into the returned position quietly. The app never produces such values, since its distances come from the path-loss formula. But a solver is a public API, and its inputs deserve the same scrutiny as its outputs. Returning an empty array on bad input is the contract both implementations share.

The story continued in 2026, while this article was being prepared. The distance function shipped in 2021 with the exponent of 2 hardcoded into the divisor, because the 4 by 6 meter test room never punished that choice. Writing the large-floor calibration recipe exposed what that hardcoding costs at deployment scale, so the exponent became the  parameter you saw in the listing, defaulting to 2 so both original call sites behave exactly as before. One commit, five years later, closing the loop between a lab measurement and a factory requirement.

Practical iBeacon Deployment: What the Radio Physics Tells You

If you are actually going to deploy BLE beacons for indoor positioning, there are practical lessons that fall out of the physics. These are not app-specific. They apply to any system that uses RSSI for distance estimation.

An iBeacon advertising packet is a BLE advertisement with a specific Apple-defined payload structure. The packet contains:

  •  (16 bytes) — a region identifier shared by a group of beacons, e.g. 07070707-0405-0607-0809-0A0B0C0D0E00. The phone filters beacons by this UUID, so all beacons in a single deployment typically share it.
  •  (2 bytes, 0–65535) — a subgroup identifier, e.g. "floor 2" or "building B."
  •  (2 bytes, 0–65535) — an individual beacon identifier within the subgroup, e.g. "beacon #14 on floor 2."
  •  (1 byte, signed) — the calibrated RSSI at 1 meter, measured at the factory. This is the  the distance formula uses. It's a starting point. You should recalibrate on-site, as I described above, because the factory value doesn't account for your specific environment.

The beacons broadcast this packet at a configurable interval, typically 100 ms (10 Hz). Shorter intervals mean more data and better responsiveness, but shorter battery life. A beacon running at 100 ms intervals on a coin cell battery will last months. At 1-second intervals, it can last over a year. For positioning, you want the shorter interval: responsiveness matters more than battery life, and beacons are usually wall-powered in permanent deployments.

Trilateration needs at least three beacons visible from any point where you want a position estimate. This sounds obvious, but achieving it in practice requires planning.

When deploying iBeacons in commercial retail facilities, office spaces, or corporate logistics warehouses, geometric placement dictates the quality of positioning. A deployment that looks reasonable on a floor plan can produce terrible results if the geometry is wrong.

The worst placement is a straight line. Three beacons along a corridor give you terrible geometry. The trilateration problem becomes ill-conditioned, and small distance errors turn into large position errors along the axis perpendicular to the line. The solver will converge, but the result will be unstable.

The best placement is a triangle: three beacons at the corners of an equilateral triangle, with the expected device position somewhere near the centroid. This gives the solver balanced constraints from multiple angles. In a rectangular room, placing beacons in three of the four corners works well. In a corridor, stagger them on opposite walls instead of putting them all on the same side.

For larger spaces, think in terms of overlapping triangles. Each area where you want positioning should have at least three beacons visible, arranged in a roughly triangular pattern. A fourth beacon adds redundancy and improves accuracy, but three well-placed beacons beat five poorly placed ones.

This is the most commonly ignored factor in indoor positioning deployments. The path-loss model assumes that the beacon and the receiver are at the same height. When they are not, the actual distance is the hypotenuse — longer than the horizontal distance — and the hypotenuse is what the RSSI responds to, whether or not your floor plan accounts for it.

If a beacon is mounted on a 3-meter ceiling and the phone is held at 1.5 meters, the vertical offset is 1.5 meters. If the horizontal distance is 2 meters, the true spatial distance is √(2² + 1.5²) ≈ 2.5 meters. The RSSI reflects 2.5 meters, but your 2D trilateration assumes 2 meters. That is a 25% error introduced purely by height mismatch.

For a 2D positioning system like BeaconIL, the solution is to mount beacons at roughly the same height as the phone, 1.5 to 2 meters, on walls rather than ceilings. This is not always practical, but it is the single biggest accuracy improvement you can make. If ceiling mounting is unavoidable, you have two options. First, correct for the height offset in software by subtracting the vertical component from the distance estimate with the Pythagorean theorem. Second, model the height explicitly: the June 2021 update made the math accept coordinates of any dimension, so each beacon can carry its mounting height and the vertical offset becomes part of the model instead of an error.

The 2.4 GHz frequency used by BLE is the same band as Wi-Fi, microwaves, and a lot of other consumer electronics. Sources of interference to watch for:

  •  — especially 802.11n/ac/ax on the 2.4 GHz band. The channels overlap with BLE advertising frequencies. Do not mount beacons within 1 meter of a Wi-Fi AP.
  •  — refrigerators, server racks, elevator shafts, metal shelving. These create strong multipath reflections. A beacon behind a metal shelf is effectively invisible.
  •  — humans are roughly 60% water, and water absorbs 2.4 GHz. A crowded environment will see RSSI drop by 3–5 dBm compared to an empty one. This is systematic, not random, so it biases distance estimates upward. There is no easy fix. The EMA filter smooths the transitions, but the bias remains.
  •  — glass is mostly transparent to 2.4 GHz, but coated or tinted glass (low-E windows) can attenuate the signal by 5–10 dBm. Drywall partitions attenuate by 2–4 dBm per wall. Concrete walls attenuate by 10–20 dBm and effectively block the signal.

The practical takeaway: calibrate in the environment where the system will operate, not in a lab. The 1-meter reference RSSI measured in an empty corridor will be different from the one measured in a warehouse full of metal shelving. BeaconIL's per-beacon calibration exists precisely for this reason.

Not Every Beacon Should Shout

The lazy instinct is to crank transmit power on every beacon. More range, more coverage, done. On a factory floor that instinct backfires. Metal everywhere, machines running, people moving: a loud beacon multiplies reflections and interference instead of coverage.  found BLE signals workable but noticeably degraded exactly there, with placement and density mattering more than raw power.

Our answer was a power ladder.

Regular beacons carried the coarse positioning layer. Some units, though, transmitted very weak signals on purpose. They became undetectable almost immediately beyond short range. Up close, after the same per-beacon calibration, their distance estimates came out close to ideal. A beacon you can only hear when you are near it tells you one thing with high confidence: that you are near it.

At the bottom rung sat near-contact emitters that behaved like NFC. Detectable within roughly ten centimeters. When a watch came that close to a guarded machine, the alarm fired on the device. Half a meter of average accuracy is fine for navigation. It is not fine as the last safety boundary near a press. Machinery safety engineering thinks in minimum separation distances between a person and a hazard zone, and an estimate with half a meter of slop cannot be that boundary. So the boundary became its own device class.

The lesson generalizes beyond factories. High transmit power is sometimes the enemy. It buys range and pays in multipath, interference, and false confidence. Weakness, used deliberately, is a feature: range collapse as a proximity signal.

What I Would Do Differently

Looking back at the code with some distance, there are things I would change.

The EMA implementation stores raw RSSI values in an array and computes the exponential average manually, shifting the array on each update. This works, but it is more complex than it needs to be. A cleaner approach would be to store only the current EMA value and the window size, applying the standard EMA formula directly: ema = α × new + (1 - α) × ema. The array-based approach was an early implementation choice that I never refactored.

The  Core Data entity stores configuration as a JSON string rather than as individual attributes. I explained the CloudKit reasoning above, and it was a deliberate trade-off. But it means you cannot use Core Data predicates to query by, say, major value. You would have to fetch all beacons and decode each one. For an app with dozens of beacons this is fine. For thousands, it would not be.

The LMA solver is a faithful port of the Apache Commons Math implementation, which means it carries over some of that code's complexity. The  and  methods are dense. They implement the Moré–Hebden algorithm for computing the LM parameter, which involves Givens rotations, rank checks, and a bracketing loop. This is correct and well-tested, but it is not code that is easy to read or maintain. A more modern approach might use a simpler trust-region method or a library like Accelerate (which is part of iOS) for the linear algebra.

What makes BeaconIL interesting is not the UI or the App Store submission. It is the math. Indoor positioning looks simple from the outside ("just use Bluetooth signals to figure out where you are") and turns out to be a rabbit hole: EMA filtering against radio noise, a path-loss model anchored by per-beacon calibration, Levenberg-Marquardt turning noisy distances into a position, thread isolation keeping BLE callbacks off the UI. Each piece is straightforward in isolation. The hard part is making them work together, in real time, on real hardware that does not behave the way textbooks say it should — and on a 4 by 6 meter test floor with three beacons, the whole chain held the estimate within about half a meter. That is the engineering challenge, and that is what made this project worth building.
