items.title: Making AI Agent Runs Reproducible, Reviewable, and Testable
items.author: Raju Dandigam
items.content:
Every generation of software has its own version of “it worked on my machine.” For AI agents, the phrase has become, “It worked on my prompt.” A developer runs an agent locally, sees a convincing answer, and assumes the system is behaving correctly. The same agent may then behave differently in a pull request, with a slightly different input, after a model update, or inside a longer workflow. The final response can still look polished even when the process behind it is wrong.

A support agent might generate an answer before retrieving the relevant policy, call the same tool twice, use an unapproved fallback, and still return plausible text. An output-only test may pass, and a flat log may contain every event, yet neither necessarily shows that the agent took an invalid path. This is not only a model-quality problem; it is an evidence problem. Teams need to know what the agent actually did, whether it followed the expected path, and whether the failing run can be shared safely for review. That is why each agent run should be treated as a reproducible, reviewable engineering artifact.

The most dangerous agent failure can still look successful

Consider a broken support-agent run. At the output boundary, the response appears acceptable: it mentions the policy, sounds helpful, and may even pass a basic text assertion.

Internally, however, the trajectory looks like this:

generate_answer          <- answered before retrieval
retrieve_policy
retrieve_policy          <- duplicate call
search_docs              <- wrong tool, failed
policyShown: failed

This is not simply a wrong-answer bug. The visible answer may be acceptable while the process violates the system design.

That distinction creates three layers of correctness:

Was the response useful, accurate, and appropriate?Human review, dataset evaluation, model grading
Did the agent use the required tools, follow an acceptable order, and complete the run?Execution facts and deterministic rules
Can another engineer inspect what happened without relying on a screenshot or exposing raw data?Portable, redacted, integrity-checked artifact

Most agent testing focuses on answer correctness, and that is reasonable because answer quality matters. However, once agents become production software, trajectory and evidence correctness matter just as much. Teams must be able to verify that the agent followed the expected path and that another engineer can independently review the run. That reviewable object is the run artifact.

Logs show events. Agents need evidence

Traditional logs are designed for event streams:

tool started
model started
tool completed
model completed
fallback used
error: timeout

This information is useful but incomplete because an agent run is not merely a list of events. It is a trajectory:

plan
→ retrieve
→ rank
→ generate
→ validate
→ maybe retry
→ maybe hand off

The order, parent-child relationships, repeated steps, and missing steps all matter. A flat log may show that ran, but not whether generation happened first, whether the second retrieval was a retry or an accidental duplicate, or whether the wrong tool appeared on an invalid branch. The final answer is only one fact about the run. Other important facts include which tools were called, in what order, whether a forbidden tool appeared, whether retrieval preceded generation, whether a required outcome passed, whether the run completed, whether a retry loop occurred, and where a good run first diverged from a bad one.

Once these become first-class facts, agent testing becomes more concrete. Semantic evaluation remains valuable for helpfulness, tone, factuality, and other open-ended qualities, but many failures are structural trajectory failures. Those failures should be testable without asking another model to judge them.

A trace is necessary, but a trace is not yet an artifact

OpenTelemetry describes a trace as a graph of spans whose parent-child relationships preserve request structure. That is a stronger foundation for agents than flat logs because an agent run is inherently hierarchical: a plan creates a tool call, the result informs a model step, and the model may trigger a retry, fallback, or handoff.

Collection, however, is only half the problem. A trace becomes a reviewable artifact through a lifecycle:

capture
→ normalize
→ inspect
→ check
→ redact
→ package
→ verify
→ attach to the work being reviewed

A trace stored in a local directory helps the person who produced it. An artifact with a stable format, summary, check results, provenance, and integrity manifest helps the next person as well. This is similar to how engineers use Playwright traces, JUnit reports, CI artifacts, coverage reports, and build logs: the failed run travels with the failure and can be archived, reopened, discussed, and compared independently of the machine that created it. For agents, this is especially important because raw runs may contain sensitive information.

LLM-as-judge evaluation is useful for questions such as whether an answer was helpful, whether its tone was appropriate, whether a summary was grounded, or whether an explanation was clear. It is not the right default for every CI gate.

Objective questions should be evaluated deterministically:

Did retrieve_policy run?
Did forbidden tool search_docs appear?
Did generation happen before retrieval?
Did the run finish?
Did a recorded outcome fail?
Did the run exceed a token or duration budget?

These are structural facts about a captured trajectory, and the same rules should produce the same result for the same trace. 

deterministic lane:
  trajectory facts, budgets, completion, safety invariants

semantic lane:
  usefulness, factual quality, preference, open-ended outcomes

The deterministic lane belongs in CI because it is inexpensive, explainable, and repeatable. The semantic lane can use model grading or human review where ambiguity justifies the additional cost and variance. A merge-blocking rule should be deliberately boring whenever the underlying question is objective.

Privacy has to be decided before the trace is shared

Agent traces may combine user messages, retrieved documents, system instructions, tool arguments, outputs, identifiers, and credentials.

This creates an important tension:

The run is the best debugging artifact.
The raw run is often the worst thing to paste into a public issue.

A safer approach separates the source trace from the shared artifact:

source trace:
  local, read-only, access-controlled

derived artifact:
  redacted, bounded, policy-assessed

manifest:
  hashes, provenance, schema, assessment

review:
  explicit human decision before sharing

Metadata-first capture can answer many trajectory questions without storing raw prompts or outputs. Tool names, step types, statuses, durations, token counts, parent relationships, and observed outcomes often explain structural drift. Redaction is still not magic: a scanner can miss context-specific secrets, and a value may become sensitive when combined with another field. Therefore, “passed the policy” should not be presented as “certified safe.” The more accurate term is a best-effort derived artifact that passed a stated local policy and still requires human review.

A minimal contract for reviewable agent runs

Before choosing a tool, define what a reviewable run artifact must guarantee. Instrumentation should preserve return values and rethrow application errors unchanged so that a tracing failure cannot become an application failure. The execution model should preserve uncertainty: if a parent-child relationship cannot be proven, it should not be invented merely to make the tree look complete; source identifiers, confidence, warnings, and unknown fields should be retained instead.

Checks must point back to evidence. “Trajectory failed” is not sufficient; a finding should identify the rule, expected fact, actual fact, and supporting event or step. The source trace and shared artifact must also remain separate objects. Redaction should create a derived copy, and packaging should never silently rewrite the trace being debugged. Verification should work offline so that a reviewer can validate the manifest and open the evidence without an account, collector, or network dependency. Finally, network behavior must be explicit: an application may call a model provider without requiring the tracing layer to upload evidence elsewhere. Capture, inspection, checking, and packaging can remain local even when the agent itself is networked.

These principles matter more than any particular CLI or SDK.

One open-source implementation of this pattern is , an MIT-licensed local evidence debugger and trajectory-testing toolkit for

TypeScript AI agents. Its focus is intentionally narrow:

local evidence for the laptop → pull request loop

It is not a hosted SaaS, production APM, prompt registry, default LLM-as-judge platform, or compliance-certification tool. Its core workflow is:

capture one local trace
→ inspect the execution tree
→ check the trajectory deterministically
→ derive a share-checked Evidence bundle
→ verify the bundle offline

The current quick start uses a synthetic, keyless demo:

npm install agent-inspect
npx agent-inspect init --yes
node examples/agent-inspect-demo.mjs
npx agent-inspect list --dir .agent-inspect

After copying a run ID, you can inspect it with:

npx agent-inspect view <run-id> --dir .agent-inspect --summary
npx agent-inspect report <run-id> --dir .agent-inspect
npx agent-inspect explain <run-id> --dir .agent-inspect

The purpose is to answer a question that logs rarely answer clearly: “What path did the agent take?”

Making the trajectory explicit

Manual instrumentation can remain small:

import { inspectRun, observeOutcome, step } from "agent-inspect";

const answer = await inspectRun(
  "support-agent",
  async () => {
    const policy = await step(
      "retrieve_policy",
      () => retrievePolicy(),
      {
        type: "tool",
        metadata: {
          toolName: "retrieve_policy",
        },
      },
    );

    const result = await step(
      "generate_answer",
      () => draftAnswer(policy),
      {
        type: "llm",
        metadata: {
          model: "your-model",
        },
      },
    );

    await observeOutcome("policyShown", {
      expectation: "The answer cites a retrieved policy",
      status: "passed",
      method: "custom",
    });

    return result;
  },
  {
    traceDir: ".agent-inspect",
  },
);

The wrapper should preserve the return value and application errors while recording the boundaries that matter. The trace does not need raw prompts or outputs to be useful. Many trajectory questions can be answered with bounded metadata such as the step name, step type, tool name, model name, duration, token counts, status, and observed outcome. That is a practical privacy default.

Turning a run into a deterministic gate

A CI check should not need another model to answer objective questions:

npx agent-inspect check <run-id> --dir .agent-inspect \
  --preset trajectory \
  --required-tool retrieve_policy \
  --forbidden-tool search_docs \
  --fail-on-observation failed

A healthy run exits ; a regression exits . An example failure might look like this:

Check status: fail
Summary: 2 failed, 0 warning(s), 0 error(s)

- outcome.status: Observed outcome count 1 matched [failed].
- tool.usage: Forbidden tool search_docs appeared.

The important properties are repeatability and explainability. A reviewer can see the concrete failed rules rather than debate the wording or consistency of a judge prompt:

forbidden tool appeared
observed outcome failed

For larger projects, the same idea can be expressed through a TraceContract-style API:

import { openTraceFile } from "agent-inspect/readers";
import {
  defineTraceContract,
  evaluateTraceContractRead,
} from "agent-inspect/checks";

const read = await openTraceFile("./.agent-inspect/demo-regression.jsonl");

const contract = defineTraceContract({
  run: {
    requireCompleted: true,
  },
  tools: {
    required: ["retrieve_policy"],
    forbidden: ["search_docs"],
  },
  observations: {
    failOn: ["failed"],
  },
});

const result = evaluateTraceContractRead(read, contract);

if (result.status !== "pass") {
  process.exitCode = 1;
}

The principle is straightforward: use deterministic checks for facts about the path and reserve model grading for semantic quality.

Evidence, not screenshots

The third requirement is collaboration. A trace that works only on one machine helps the author; a trace that another engineer can review helps the team.

AgentInspect’s bundle flow derives a review artifact from the local trace:

npx agent-inspect verify-safe <run-id> --dir .agent-inspect

npx agent-inspect bundle <run-id> --dir .agent-inspect \
  --profile share \
  --out ./evidence

npx agent-inspect bundle verify ./evidence

The derived folder can include:

evidence.html          offline review surface
evidence.json          manifest and SHA-256 file hashes
trace.jsonl            redacted derived trace
check-results.json     deterministic findings
redaction-report.json  detector summary without secret values
summary.md             human-readable overview

checks the manifest, listed files, hashes, assessment, and provenance offline. This is not a cryptographic signature or compliance guarantee; it is an integrity check for a local derived artifact. The source trace remains local, while the bundle can be attached to a pull request, incident thread, or internal review.

Why TypeScript needs its own layer

Much AI tooling began in Python, but TypeScript agent development has its own requirements, including Node.js async context, ESM and CommonJS boundaries, serverless and edge runtimes, the Vercel AI SDK, OpenAI Agents JS, LangChain.js and LangGraph, Vitest and Jest workflows, and MCP clients and coding assistants. A useful TypeScript debugging tool must fit that ecosystem rather than assume every run is a Python script or notebook.

AgentInspect supports several capture paths:

These capture paths feed the same workflow:

capture
→ inspect
→ check
→ bundle
→ verify

Local evidence and hosted observability solve different problems

This approach is not an argument against hosted observability. Hosted systems are well suited to production dashboards, long-term retention, team-wide trace search, hosted datasets, alerting, large-scale evaluation management, prompt registries, and fleet metrics. A local evidence layer serves a different purpose: fast local debugging, pull-request gates, share-checked incident artifacts, private or regulated traces, offline review, and coding-assistant access to local run facts.

The two layers can coexist. A useful analogy is:

git locally
code host remotely

Local history and hosted collaboration serve different purposes, and agent evidence can follow the same pattern.

What the artifact does not prove

A well-structured run can still produce a bad answer, a green trajectory check can encode the wrong requirement, and a redacted bundle can still contain context-specific information that a generic detector missed. The artifact does not prove that the answer was factually correct, that the user achieved the desired real-world outcome, that every policy was modeled as a rule, that production behavior matches a fixture, that the evidence meets a legal or compliance standard, or that the system is safe without human review.

Its value is narrower and more practical:

the run is inspectable
the structural expectations are executable
the review handoff depends less on memory and screenshots

That is enough to improve engineering practice without pretending to solve agent reliability in a single layer.

A practical test for your current agent stack

Take one known-bad run and ask whether you can reconstruct the execution tree without reading timestamps line by line, identify the first divergence from a known-good run, assert required and forbidden tool behavior without another model call, block a pull request with a stable exit code, produce a redacted copy without mutating the source trace, open the artifact offline, verify which files were packaged and whether they changed, and explain exactly when any data leaves the machine.

If several answers are “no,” the team may have telemetry but not yet have a reviewable run artifact. The next step is not necessarily a new platform. Preserve one failure, write three structural invariants, and attach the evidence to the change that fixes it.

If you build TypeScript agents and want to test this workflow, the keyless starter is the fastest path:

npm install agent-inspect
npx agent-inspect init --yes
node examples/agent-inspect-demo.mjs
npx agent-inspect list --dir .agent-inspect

If the project is useful or not useful yet, specific feedback is valuable:

This framework adapter is missing.
This command was confusing.
This trace did not preserve the structure I needed.
This CI rule would make it useful for my team.
This evidence artifact needs a different field.

Documentation improvements, fixtures, framework recipes, and good first issues are welcome.

From prompt demo to engineering evidence

“It worked on my prompt” describes a successful moment, not a reproducible system. An agent becomes easier to trust when its run can be inspected as a tree, checked as a trajectory, and reviewed as an artifact. Semantic evaluation and production observability still matter; the missing discipline is making the individual run durable enough to connect them.

Keep one known-bad run, turn its failure path into deterministic rules, and package the evidence a second engineer would need to review the fix. If that workflow is difficult, you have found a concrete tooling gap, not another prompt to tweak.

items.title: Building Reusable Evidence for AI Governance Frameworks
items.author: Prasenjit
items.content:
AI governance can become complicated very quickly.

One team works with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Another prepares for the EU AI Act. A third is building an ISO/IEC 42001 management system. Legal, security, data and engineering may each maintain separate control lists. The result is often more governance paperwork, but not necessarily better governance.

There is a simpler way to think about it:

Build the control once. Generate the evidence once. Map that evidence to multiple requirements.

Three Frameworks, Different Purposes

NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act and ISO/IEC 42001 are not interchangeable.

The NIST AI RMF provides a voluntary risk-management structure built around four functions:

Govern -> Map -> Measure -> Manage

The EU AI Act establishes legal obligations. For high-risk AI systems, Articles 9 through 15 address areas such as risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.

ISO/IEC 42001 provides a management-system structure for governing AI across an organization. It specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an Artificial Intelligence Management System.

The mistake teams make is building three separate sets of technical controls. Instead, separate the requirement from the control and from the evidence.

One Control Can Produce Evidence for Several Regimes

An AI system may need controls for:

    The same evidence may support NIST AI RMF activities, EU AI Act data-governance requirements and ISO/IEC 42001 operational controls. The requirements remain different.

    The evidence can be reused when it is relevant and properly mapped. The same principle applies across the AI lifecycle.

    Risk assessment and harm mapping

    NIST Govern and Map; EU AI Act Article 9

    Quality record and lineage report

    NIST Map and Measure; EU AI Act Article 10; ISO/IEC 42001 operations

    System and decision logging

    NIST Measure; EU AI Act Article 12

    Human review and escalation

    NIST Manage; EU AI Act Article 14

    Drift, bias and performance monitoring

    Evaluation reports and alerts

    NIST Measure and Manage; EU AI Act Article 15

    Incident and change management

    Incident reports, change records and corrective actions

    NIST Govern and Manage; ISO/IEC 42001 improvement processes

    This is where governance starts becoming an engineering discipline rather than a documentation exercise.

    Logging Should Be Part of the Architecture

    A policy can say that decisions must be traceable. That does not make a decision traceable. The platform needs to capture the evidence required to reconstruct what happened.

    For an AI-assisted decision, useful evidence may include:

    • Decision taken & Human review
    This is why observability and governance increasingly overlap.

    A well-designed AI platform should not require teams to reconstruct its history months later from spreadsheets, emails and meeting notes. The evidence should already exist. For high-risk AI systems, the EU AI Act requires systems to technically allow the automatic recording of relevant events over the system's lifetime.

    Human Oversight Needs a Workflow

    "Human in the loop" is often written into AI governance policies and the more useful question is what that person can actually do.

    • Can the reviewer inspect the result?
    • Can the reviewer reject it?
    • Can the reviewer override it?
    • Can the case be escalated?
    • Is that decision recorded?

    Human oversight becomes meaningful when it is implemented as a system capability rather than a sentence in a policy.

    Review -> Approve -> Override -> Escalate -> Record

    That workflow can provide evidence for several governance and regulatory requirements.

    Governance programs often devote significant effort to policies, committees, inventories and assessments and those activities matter but AI risk also needs to be measured in production.

    • What happens when model performance falls below a threshold?
    • What happens when drift increases?
    • What happens when data quality deteriorates?
    • What happens when an exception rate becomes unacceptable?

    A mature system should connect monitoring to action.

    Threshold -> Alert -> Review -> Action -> Evidence

    That may mean intervention, rollback, retraining, restriction or retirement and without that operational loop, governance can describe risk without actually controlling it.

    Build Controls Around Risk, Not Regulation

    Regulations and standards will continue to evolve and building a new technical control every time a requirement changes are difficult to sustain.

    A stronger approach is to create durable controls around the underlying risks:

      Then maintain mappings that show how those controls satisfy or support different requirements. The regulatory map may change but the underlying engineering controls should be far more stable and that is the central idea: Do not build a control for every framework! Build a strong control, generate reliable evidence and map that evidence wherever it is required.

      [1] National Institute of Standards and Technology, "AI Risk Management Framework," NIST.

      [2] European Parliament and Council of the European Union, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, "Artificial Intelligence Act," Articles 9-15.

      [3] International Organization for Standardization, "ISO/IEC 42001:2023 - Information technology - Artificial intelligence - Management system."

items.title: The Inventions and Pioneers That Built Podcasting
items.author: Cameron Stack
items.content:
Podcasting wasn’t invented in 2004.

It was built on more than a century of inventions, discoveries, experiments, and ideas.

The microphone, radio, magnetic tape, stereo, digital audio, MP3, RSS, and the iPod all existed before podcasting emerged. Each generation stood on the work of the one before it.

Isaac Newton famously wrote, “If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants.” Podcasting is a similar story.

The people behind its evolution came from very different fields. Inventors, engineers, broadcasters, mathematicians, software developers, entrepreneurs, and journalists all contributed pieces of the technology and infrastructure that eventually made podcasting possible.

This is a selection of the people every podcaster should know, and the contributions that helped make modern podcasting possible.

  •  (1881–1945) was a German-Austrian engineer who patented magnetic recording tape in 1928. Magnetic tape allowed recorded audio to be edited, spliced, and re-recorded, and it became a standard medium for sound production. [Wikipedia: Fritz Pfleumer]
  •  (1903–1942) was a British electronics engineer who, in 1931, patented a system of binaural, or stereophonic, sound, describing methods for recording and reproducing sound in two channels. He was regarded as one of the most significant engineers and inventors of his time and held 128 patents.
    • In 2017, the Recording Academy posthumously awarded Alan Dower Blumlein the Technical Grammy for the invention of stereo and contributions of outstanding technical significance to the recording field.
  •  (born 1931) is a German physicist who, with, invented the foil electret microphone at Bell Labs in 1962. Electret microphones became the most widely produced type of microphone, used in telephones, computers, and hearing aids. Together with Dietmar Hohm, he also invented the MEMS microphone, which is common in modern devices like smartphones, earbuds, and smartwatches.
  •  (1856–1943) was a Serbian-American inventor and engineer whose experiments with alternating current, high-frequency electricity, and wireless transmission helped establish technologies that would later underpin radio communication. In the 1890s, Tesla demonstrated the transmission of electrical signals without physical wires and developed tuned circuits that allowed wireless signals to be selectively transmitted and received. His work helped establish important principles behind wireless communication, which eventually made it possible to transmit sound through radio rather than a physical connection.
  •  (1874–1937) was an Italian inventor and electrical engineer credited with developing long-distance radio transmission. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Karl Ferdinand Braun.
  •  (1866–1932) was a Canadian-American inventor who is often credited with making the first audio radio broadcast, transmitting voice and music on 24 December 1906, at a time when radio was used primarily for Morse code.
  •  (1873–1961) was an American inventor who patented the Audion, a triode vacuum tube, in 1906 (with the initial detector patent granted in 1907 and the triode patent in 1908). The device could amplify weak electrical signals and became fundamental to radio, telephone, and later electronic sound systems. De Forest conducted early experimental broadcasts and is sometimes called the “father of radio.”
  •  (1875–1948) was an American inventor and broadcaster. He began experimental voice transmissions in San Jose, California, in 1909 and, from 1912, made regularly scheduled broadcasts of music and speech to an audience. His station later became KCBS. He is often described as one of the first people to make regular broadcasts to the public.
  •  (1889–1976) and (1916–2001) were engineers and mathematicians whose work established the sampling theorem, which describes how a continuous signal can be represented by discrete samples. The theorem is a foundation of digital audio and is fundamental to how digital systems record and reproduce sound. [Wikipedia: Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem]
  •  (born 1954) is a German electrical engineer who led development of the MP3 audio compression format at the Fraunhofer Institute. MP3 reduced the file size of digital audio, making it practical to store and distribute over the internet, and it remains a common format for podcast distribution. [Wikipedia: MP3]
  • There was no single precursor or single person responsible. Creators, technologists, and companies were independently exploring ways to produce, distribute, and consume audio outside traditional broadcasting. The 2000 collaboration between Don Katz, Robin Williams, and Audible is one example. It demonstrated that original audio could be delivered automatically to a portable device years before RSS-based podcasting emerged. It was not a podcast in the modern technical sense, but it demonstrated an important part of the idea behind podcasting.
  •  (born 1955) is an American software developer known for his work on RSS. Around 2000 and 2001 he added support for enclosures, which allow a media file to be attached to an item in an RSS feed so that subscribing software can download it automatically. This mechanism is the technical basis of podcasting. [Wikipedia: History of podcasting]
  •  is a writer and technologist who, in 2000, proposed attaching media files to RSS feeds, an idea subsequently implemented by Winer.
  •  is a software engineer who, at the first BloggerCon conference in 2003, demonstrated a script that downloaded audio enclosures from RSS feeds and transferred them to an iPod.
  •  (born 1940) is an American journalist and radio host. In 2003, while a fellow at Harvard’s Berkman Center, he recorded a series of interviews distributed using RSS enclosures. His interview with Winer in July 2003 is often cited as the first podcast. His program, later titled , is among the longest-running podcasts. [Wired: First Podcast Oral History]
  •  (born 1964) is an American broadcaster and former MTV VJ. He worked with Winer to develop iPodder, software that automatically downloaded audio enclosures, and launched the  podcast in 2004. He is frequently referred to as the “Podfather.” In 2020, with Dave Jones, he launched Podcast Index, an open podcast directory, and the Podcasting 2.0 initiative, which proposed additions to the RSS specification such as transcripts, chapters, and listener payments. [Podnews: Podcasting 20th Birthday]
  •  is a British journalist who, in a February 2004 article for , suggested “podcasting” as a name for the emerging medium of downloadable audio. The term was widely adopted.
  •  was a podcasting pioneer who is credited with suggesting the term  to Dave Winer and Adam Curry in 2004, helping give the emerging medium its name.
  •  (1955–2011) was the co-founder and chief executive of Apple. In June 2005, under his leadership, Apple added podcast support to its iTunes software, including a directory of available podcasts. The addition increased the accessibility and popularity of podcasts, and for many years the iTunes directory served as a primary means of discovering them. [Apple Newsroom: 2005]
  •  (1964–2025) was an American podcaster and businessman. He hosted , wrote an early guide to podcasting in 2005, and founded RawVoice and Blubrry, companies providing podcast hosting, measurement, and advertising services, as well as the (commonly the) in 2005; the first ceremony was held in 2006. The Podcast Awards are widely described as the first and longest-running podcast-specific awards open globally. He was inducted into the Podcast Hall of Fame in 2015. He died on 8 September 2025. [Todd Cochrane obituary] [Wikipedia: Podcast Awards] [Podcast Awards]
  •  (born 1956) is an American broadcaster who launched the technology podcast  in 2005 and founded the TWiT.tv network, one of the earliest professional podcast networks.

items.title: The Explainability Problem in AI Payment Systems
items.author: Sergei Magas
items.content:
Nvidia shares jumped nearly 5% in after-hours trading after the company reported quarterly revenue that more than doubled year-over-year, with data center revenue surging 117%. Nvidia’s outlook reinforced expectations that AI infrastructure spending remains robust, with the company projecting revenue growth of approximately 70% for the 2028 fiscal year.

The results provided a fresh boost to the broader technology sector, which had faced pressure in recent sessions due to rising bond yields and concerns that high valuations left little margin for error regarding earnings.

Last week, Indian company Razorpay announced the launch of Razorpay Vulcan—India’s first AI Transformer model built specifically for payments, per the announcement. The model combines Razorpay’s payment data with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AWS cloud infrastructure, including Amazon SageMaker.

For millions of local shoppers, a single failed transaction, a delayed OTP, or a fraudulent charge is reason enough to revert to cash. As the country’s e-commerce market heads toward a projected $250 billion by 2030, the reliability of digital payments has become an economic priority. Razorpay, in collaboration with NVIDIA and AWS, has addressed this challenge with a unified AI model that evaluates all possible payment routes in real time and selects the most reliable one before the transaction is attempted.

Fintech investors have reacted positively to this news, and at first glance, rightly so. Yet, beneath these impressive metrics lies a risk that has not yet been factored into any analyst report.

The Flip Side of Accuracy

For the fintech sector, such a development can be a double-edged sword. Increasing model accuracy entails not only reduced fraud-related costs but also more legitimate users facing automatic transaction rejections. At a scale of billions of transactions, even a fractional error rate translates into hundreds of thousands of real customers and businesses facing rejection or account blocking without a clear explanation. This often occurs because the decision exists merely as internal model weights rather than a human-readable rule that could be explained to a support agent or the customer themselves.

As Vadim Drozd, CEO of payment infrastructure company FinteqHub, notes: "When a system is five times more accurate at catching disputed transactions, it’s a great metric for a boardroom report, but it's very bad news for the individual user whose legitimate payment the model mistakenly classified as an anomaly and who now faces a denial without a clear explanation, because the only explanation exists in the form of a vector of weights within the transformer." In his view, it is precisely this scale — billions of transactions annually — that transforms a statistically insignificant model error into a systemic trust issue for the entire industry.

This creates a precedent familiar from other sectors. A similar trajectory was seen in the regulation of algorithmic decision-making within lending and hiring, where model opacity eventually led to demands for a right to an explanation — first under the EU’s GDPR and later in US industry standards. While this regulatory wave has not yet fully hit the payments sector, the market is already grappling with a rising volume of complaints about increasing regulatory scrutiny of algorithmic transparency in financial services and a broader trend toward stricter requirements for AI explainability within critical infrastructure.

Who is directly affected?

For investors holding positions in PayPal, Block, or Adyen, or eyeing Razorpay’s future IPO, this implies a cost item not yet factored into margin models. Companies currently investing in such a transparency gateway will gain a structural advantage in terms of customer trust and will likely be less vulnerable to future regulatory demands. Conversely, those optimizing solely for accuracy and success rates risk a delayed hit to their reputation and a regulatory-driven capital expenditure spike 12–18 months down the line — precisely when the market expects margin growth acceleration rather than new compliance costs.

AI accuracy in payments is a real and measurable driver of short-term revenue growth. However, explainability risk represents an asymmetric downside that the market systematically underestimates — precisely because it does not show up in quarterly reports until the first high-profile regulatory action or legal precedent occurs. A prudent strategy is to look beyond the players demonstrating the best AI accuracy metrics and focus on those who are already embedding explainability and human oversight into their product architecture.

items.title: 1.89 Seasons: A Baseball Experiment About Hiring and Human Judgment
items.author: Elodie Aishwarya P. Remoissenet
items.content:
Nearly every evaluation system in wide use answers the same question: how does this person compare to people like them? Years of experience, school, sector, title trajectory. A statistical claim about a category, applied to an individual who happens to be standing inside it. I have spent this year arguing that the hierarchy is backwards: the population is a prior, not a verdict, and its weight should move as an individual's own evidence accumulates. This week I stopped arguing and measured.

Not on hiring data, because there is no public hiring data worth the name: I could not find a single public dataset with the repeated, standardized, outcome-linked observations this test requires. So I went to a large public dataset that has exactly that: the Lahman Baseball Database, season by season, the licensed statistical record of a public profession. Baseball is also where a version of this argument played out at scale once before, when the individual record beat the scouting category badly enough that the sport reorganized around the result. If a claim about estimators survives in front of that audience, it survives anywhere.

The question, in one sentence

Predict a player's next season twice. Once from his own prior seasons only, identity kept, category discarded. Once from the mean of his reference class, age, position, era, playing time, category kept, identity discarded. At what number of prior observations does the individual model overtake the categorical one, out of sample? Call that number n*.

Honesty about the neighborhood first, because it is crowded. Under squared error, n* and the classical shrinkage weight are one object: reliability equals one half exactly at the crossing. Sabermetrics has published reliability curves for years, and empirical Bayes has blended individual histories with population priors since James-Stein. The psychology of it is a century old, idiographic against nomothetic, and the non-ergodicity literature has shown that group statistics generalize poorly to individuals. What I could not find anywhere was the empirical crossing measured against its analytic prediction, on real data, framed as the decision rule a selection system actually needs, with the direction of the gap stated before running. So that is what the pilot does.

The numbers, with their conditions welded on

Design: three estimators, the reference class fitted leave-self-out, a Marcel-class blend as the honest third party, strict rolling-origin validation, 32 origins, test seasons 1991 to 2022, roughly 11,500 held-out cases per metric.

The analytic prediction for OPS, from the variance components alone, says the individual should win after 1.21 prior seasons. The measured crossing lands at , 95% cluster-bootstrap interval [1.71, 2.15], at a 100 plate-appearance exposure floor. The gap is +0.68 seasons, and its sign, later than the analytic value, was written down before the run. For strikeout rate, a fast-stabilizing skill, the individual wins from the first observed season in every variant tested.

Two conditions are not footnotes, they are part of the number. The crossing is an upper bound: players who collapse leave the sample, and they are exactly the ones the reference class misses most, so censoring inflates the crossing, and a decensoring sweep walks it from 1.89 down toward 1.44. And the gap is floor-conditional, shrinking from +0.69 at a 50 PA floor to +0.25 at 300. House rule, printed in the repository: quote the crossing with its floor or not at all.

What broke, and what it taught

I ran an adversarial audit against my own pipeline before believing it, and the audit reversed my favorite explanation. I had attributed the gap to the reference class being well conditioned on age, position and playing time. Measured contribution: about 0.09 of the 0.68. Roughly half turned out to be era drift: variance components fitted on 1954 to 1990 no longer describe 1991 to 2022. The category is not just the wrong denominator, it is a denominator estimated on yesterday's population. If that sentence sounds like it is about hiring, that is because it is.

The rest sits on the individual's side, and it is the finding I did not plan. Aging. A veteran's long history overweights his own peak, so the fitted weight on the individual record climbs to about 0.90 by six prior seasons and then slides back under the analytic curve, while for a stable skill like strikeout rate it climbs toward 0.97 and never slides. The static shrinkage model used here has no term for either effect. Within this sport, n* tracks the signal-to-noise of the metric, not the metric's prestige.

the pilot has since been independently reproduced from the public repository in a clean environment by Maxime Baelde, one command, checksum verified, exact match on both headline numbers, 1.21 analytic and 1.89 empirical. His reading then turns the pilot's own sensitivity data against the pooled gap: per-era residuals of +0.47 (1991 to 2006) and +0.28 (2007 to 2022), bracketing the fit-window component at a third to two thirds of the headline +0.68, a sharper cut than the rough half reported above, and he presses the stationarity assumption harder than this paper does. A critique, not an endorsement, public in full: github.com/labs-barkley/irep-crossing-point/issues/1

One more honesty, visible in the figures: the blend beats both pure estimators everywhere. That is not an embarrassment, it is the operational conclusion. The crossing tells you when the individual dominates the category; the fitted weight tells you how to mix them at any n. For a real selection system the deliverable is a weight, not a winner.

So what does baseball have to do with hiring?

Quite a lot, once you see that the problem is neither baseball nor hiring but reference classes. A résumé is built almost entirely from category variables: degree, employer, title, sector, years. Each one is a population prior, a statement about what people in that box tend to do, applied to an individual before their own record has been allowed to speak. Baseball simply happens to be a public arena where both estimators can be run against real outcomes across 69 seasons.

That is the proxy trap. Hiring measures what is easy to standardize, school, title, employer, tenure, and gradually mistakes those proxies for the capability it wanted to observe. The résumé makes it worse: it compresses a longitudinal person into categorical snapshots, and what someone built, learned, repaired or repeatedly delivered becomes harder to see than the boxes they passed through. So the question shifts, from compared to whom toward compared to when: what does this individual's own trajectory say, once enough of it exists to be informative?

The transfer is therefore not empirical, it is structural. This pilot does not say that 1.89 seasons equals 1.89 jobs, and anyone quoting it that way is misreading it. What travels is the geometry: the weight assigned to the category should move as the individual's own evidence accumulates, and when the population itself drifts, the category fails twice, because it describes other people, and it describes them from another time.

The mechanism may travel. The number does not.

What this does and does not say about hiring

It asks the question, it does not answer it. Baseball supplies hundreds of observations per subject; a hiring file supplies about three. Nothing here validates any hiring protocol, and the causal question, whether hiring under an individual-referential protocol produces better hires, is a different question with its own literature. The sharpest treatment of it is not mine: Maxime Baelde's structural analysis of the IREP validation plan (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22112323) shows exactly what that causal claim would take, and the protocol has absorbed it in public, issue by issue.

This pilot generates hypotheses; it does not confirm them. They are now frozen, on the record, for a confirmatory second domain with a different noise structure. If the same geometry holds there, the claim graduates. If it does not, that gets published too.

Everything reproduces in one command, from raw download to figures, numpy and matplotlib and nothing else: github.com/labs-barkley/irep-crossing-point, archived as DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22125148. The protocol it tests lives at irepprotocol.org (working paper DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21211589).

The résumé is a compression algorithm that discards exactly the signal that now matters. 1.89 seasons is not hiring's number. It is the first measured version of the question hiring has not yet had the data to ask: how much of a person's own record does it take before the category should give way.

I am proudly AI-assisted. This piece was originally written in French. AI tools were used for translation, proofreading, and structural editing. The ideas, arguments, examples, experiences, original French draft, and vision remain my own.

produced by the study pipeline itself (matplotlib, one command from raw data to charts, reproducible from the repository). Any brand cards shown are AI-assisted design work.

items.title: From Archive to Story: Character-Consistent Image Pipelines with Gemini Nano Banana
items.author: Laurent Picard
items.content:
ℹ️ The complete source code is available in this notebook (including setup details and future updates) under the Apache 2.0 license. You can also directly open the notebook in Colab. This article reproduces the results from running the notebook.

We all have existing images worth reusing in different contexts. Doing so typically involves modifying the images, a complex (if not impossible) task requiring very specific skills and tools. This explains why our archives are full of forgotten or unused treasures. State-of-the-art vision models have evolved so much that we can reconsider this problem.

So, can we breathe new life into our visual archives?

Let's take on this challenge with the following steps:

  • 1️⃣ Start with an archive image we'd like to reuse
  • 2️⃣ Extract a character to create a brand-new reference image
  • 3️⃣ Generate a series of images to illustrate the character's journey, using only prompts and the new assets

For this, we'll explore the capabilities of Nano Banana 🍌.

We'll use the following packages:

  •  for request management (a dependency of )
  •  and  for data visualization (dependencies of )
pip install --quiet "google-genai>=2.12.1" "networkx[default]"

To send Gemini requests, we'll use a  client:

from google import genai

client = genai.Client()

For this challenge, we'll select the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (Nano Banana 2 Lite) model, the fastest and cheapest in the Nano Banana family:

  • NANO_BANANA_MODEL = "gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image"

Now, let's define some helper functions to generate and display images:

import IPython.display
import tenacity
from google.genai.errors import ClientError
from google.genai.types import GenerateContentConfig, ImageConfig, PIL_Image

NANO_BANANA_MODEL = "gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image"

# You can add the "TEXT" modality for potential textual feedback (or in iterative chat mode)
RESPONSE_MODALITIES = ["IMAGE"]

# Supported aspect ratios: 1:1, 1:4, 4:1, 1:8, 8:1, 2:3, 3:2, 3:4, 4:3, 4:5, 5:4, 9:16, 16:9, 21:9
ASPECT_RATIO = "16:9"

GENERATION_CONFIG = GenerateContentConfig(
    response_modalities=RESPONSE_MODALITIES,
    image_config=ImageConfig(
        aspect_ratio=ASPECT_RATIO,
        image_size="1K",
        output_mime_type="image/png" if client.vertexai else None,
    ),
)


def generate_content(sources: list[PIL_Image], prompt: str) -> PIL_Image | None:
    prompt = prompt.strip()
    contents = [*sources, prompt] if sources else prompt

    response = None
    for attempt in get_retrier():
        with attempt:
            response = client.models.generate_content(
                model=NANO_BANANA_MODEL,
                contents=contents,
                config=GENERATION_CONFIG,
            )

    if not response or not response.candidates:
        return None
    if not (content := response.candidates[0].content):
        return None
    if not (parts := content.parts):
        return None

    image: PIL_Image | None = None
    for part in parts:
        if part.text:
            display_markdown(part.text)
            continue
        assert (sdk_image := part.as_image())
        assert (image := sdk_image._pil_image)
        display_image(image)

    return image


def get_retrier() -> tenacity.Retrying:
    return tenacity.Retrying(
        stop=tenacity.stop_after_attempt(7),
        wait=tenacity.wait_incrementing(start=10, increment=1),
        retry=tenacity.retry_if_exception(should_retry_request),
        reraise=True,
    )


def should_retry_request(err: BaseException) -> bool:
    if not isinstance(err, ClientError):
        return False
    print(f"❌ ClientError {err.code}: {err.message}")

    retry = False
    match err.code:
        case 400 if err.message is not None and " try again " in err.message:
            # Workshop: project accessing Cloud Storage for the first time (service agent provisioning)
            retry = True
        case 429:
            # Workshop: temporary project with 1 QPM quota
            retry = True
    print(f"🔄 Retry: {retry}")

    return retry


def display_markdown(markdown: str) -> None:
    IPython.display.display(IPython.display.Markdown(markdown))


def display_image(image: PIL_Image) -> None:
    IPython.display.display(image)

Let's define the assets for our character's journey and the functions to manage them:

import enum
from collections.abc import Sequence
from dataclasses import dataclass


class AssetId(enum.StrEnum):
    ARCHIVE = "0_archive"
    ROBOT = "1_robot"
    MOUNTAINS = "2_mountains"
    VALLEY = "3_valley"
    FOREST = "4_forest"
    CLEARING = "5_clearing"
    ASCENSION = "6_ascension"
    SUMMIT = "7_summit"
    BRIDGE = "8_bridge"
    HAMMOCK = "9_hammock"


@dataclass
class Asset:
    id: str
    source_ids: Sequence[str]
    prompt: str
    pil_image: PIL_Image


class Assets(dict[str, Asset]):
    def set_asset(self, asset: Asset) -> None:
        # Note: This replaces any existing asset (if needed, add guardrails to auto-save or keep all versions)
        self[asset.id] = asset


def generate_image(source_ids: Sequence[str], prompt: str, new_id: str = "") -> None:
    sources = [assets[source_id].pil_image for source_id in source_ids]
    prompt = prompt.strip()
    image = generate_content(sources, prompt)
    if image and new_id:
        assets.set_asset(Asset(new_id, source_ids, prompt, image))


assets = Assets()

We can now fetch our reference archive and make it our first asset:

import urllib.request
from io import BytesIO

import PIL.Image

ARCHIVE_URL = "https://storage.googleapis.com/github-repo/generative-ai/gemini/use-cases/media-generation/consistent_imagery_generation/0_archive.png"


def load_archive() -> None:
    image = get_image_from_url(ARCHIVE_URL)
    assets.set_asset(Asset(AssetId.ARCHIVE, [], "", image))
    display_image(image)


def get_image_from_url(image_url: str) -> PIL_Image:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(image_url, timeout=10) as response:
        return PIL.Image.open(BytesIO(response.read()))


load_archive()

ℹ️ This archive image was generated in July 2024 with a beta version of Imagen 3, using the prompt "On a white background, a small hand-felted toy of a blue robot. The felt is soft and cuddly […]". The result looked really good, but there was absolutely no determinism or consistency at the time. This was a nice one-shot generation, and the cute little robot seemed lost forever…

Let's try to extract our little robot:

source_ids = [AssetId.ARCHIVE]
prompt = "Convert everything but the robot to pure white pixels."

generate_image(source_ids, prompt)

⚠️ The robot is extracted perfectly, but this is essentially just a good background-removal job (something many dedicated machine learning models can do). This prompt uses terms from graphics software, whereas we can now think in terms of image composition. It's also not necessarily a good idea to use traditional binary masks, as object edges and shadows convey significant details about shapes, textures, positions, and lighting.

Let's go back to our archive to perform an advanced extraction instead and directly generate a character sheet…

Gemini has spatial understanding, so it can provide different views while preserving visual features. Let's generate a front/back character sheet and add a backpack at the same time, since our little robot is going on a journey:

source_ids = [AssetId.ARCHIVE]
prompt = """
- Scene: Character sheet of the robot, based on the provided image.
- Setting: Isolated on a pure white background, razor-sharp focus, vibrant saturated colors, bright studio lighting.
- Left Side: Straight-on front view of the robot wearing a small backpack made of warm chocolate-brown suede, with thin, matching straps around the shoulders.
- Right Side: Straight-on back view of the robot wearing the same backpack. The backpack's flap is secured by a tiny, matte-brass, rounded-square ring buckle. The back of the robot's head must be completely seamless.
- Text: Small sans-serif text. Centered at the top, a caption "ROBOT CHARACTER SHEET". At the bottom, label the left side "FRONT VIEW" and the right side "BACK VIEW".
"""
new_id = AssetId.ROBOT

generate_image(source_ids, prompt, new_id)
  • Our prompt focuses on the composition of the scene, a common practice in media studios.
  • Repeated generations will be consistent, preserving all robot features visible in the provided image. However, since we only described a few features of the backpack (e.g., a single buckle) and left the rest open to interpretation, we'll get slightly different backpacks.
  • For simplicity, we directly included the backpack in the character sheet. In a real production pipeline, we would likely make it part of a separate accessory sheet.
  • To control the backpack's exact shape and design, we could also use a reference photo of a real backpack and instruct Gemini to "transform the backpack into a stylized felt version."
  • Nano Banana 2 Lite can generate  images ( pixels at the  aspect ratio) or equivalent resolutions (token-wise) for other supported aspect ratios (, , , , , , , , , , , , and ). Larger Nano Banana models can generate  or  images.
  • In the request configuration, we specified , which generates images at  pixels. If this parameter is omitted, Gemini uses the aspect ratio of the input image (the last one if multiple are provided) to select the closest supported aspect ratio.

This new asset can now serve as a design reference for our future image-generation tasks.

Let's get started with a mountain scene:

source_ids = [AssetId.ROBOT]
prompt = """
- Image 1: Reference robot character sheet.
- Scene: Macro photography of a beautifully crafted miniature diorama.
- Background: Soft focus on an infinite panoramic range of interspersed, dome-like smooth-felt mountains, in random shades of medium blue/green, all with curvy white snowcaps, extending over the entire horizon.
- Foreground: On the bottom left, the robot stands on the edge of a medium-gray felt cliff, captured from a 3/4 rear view, looking out over a sea of clouds (made of white cotton).
- Lighting: Studio, warm, clean and soft.
"""
new_id = AssetId.MOUNTAINS

generate_image(source_ids, prompt, new_id)

💡 The mountain shape is specified as "dome-like", so our character can stand on one of the summits later on.

It's important to spend some time on this first scene, as it will have a cascading effect that defines the overall look of our story. Don't hesitate to refine the prompt or run it a couple of times to get your preferred variation.

From now on, our generation inputs will typically include the character sheet for consistency, along with a previous scene to provide context for the next step…

Let's get the robot down into a valley:

source_ids = [AssetId.ROBOT, AssetId.MOUNTAINS]
prompt = """
- Image 1: Reference robot character sheet.
- Image 2: Previous scene.
- The robot has descended from the cliff into a gray felt valley. It stands in the center, seen directly from the back. It is holding/reading a felt map.
- Large, smooth, round felt rocks in various beige/gray shades are visible on the sides.
- Background: The distant infinite panoramic mountain range extending over the entire horizon. A thin layer of clouds obscures its base and the end of the valley.
- Lighting: Golden hour light, soft and diffused.
"""
new_id = AssetId.VALLEY

generate_image(source_ids, prompt, new_id)
  • The specific references to our input images ( and ) are important. Without them, "the robot" could refer to any of the three robots in the input images (two in the character sheet, one in the previous scene). With them, we indicate that it is the same robot. To prevent confusion (or if the model gets confused), we can be more specific with "the [entity] from image [number]".
  • On the other hand, since we didn't provide a precise description of the valley, repeated requests will produce different, interesting, and creative results (we can pick our favorite or make the prompt more precise for greater determinism).
  • Here, we also tested different lighting, which significantly changes the whole scene.

Then, we can move forward with the story:

source_ids = [AssetId.ROBOT, AssetId.VALLEY]
prompt = """
- Image 1: Reference robot character sheet.
- Image 2: Previous scene.
- The robot continues its journey through the valley and faces a dense wall of giant, thin trees hiding the entire background.
- The trees are made of light/medium/dark green felt.
- The robot is on the right, seen from a 3/4 rear angle, looking up at the trees. It is no longer holding the map. Instead, its arms are raised beside its ears.
- In the bottom-left and bottom-right corners, rocks (similar to Image 2) are partially visible.
"""
new_id = AssetId.FOREST

generate_image(source_ids, prompt, new_id)
  • We can position the character, change its point of view, and even "animate" its arms for more expressiveness.
  • The "no longer holding the map" instruction prevents the model from carrying it over from the previous scene in an awkward or unwanted way (like having the robot drop the map on the ground).
  • Since we didn't provide lighting details, the light source, quality, and direction are preserved from the previous scene.

Let's go through the forest:

source_ids = [AssetId.ROBOT, AssetId.FOREST]
prompt = """
- Image 1: Reference robot character sheet.
- Image 2: Previous scene.
- The robot walks through the dense forest and emerges into a clearing, making its way between two trees.
- The robot is in the center, now seen from the front.
- The ground is made of green felt, with flat patches of white felt snow. Rocks are no longer visible.
"""
new_id = AssetId.CLEARING

generate_image(source_ids, prompt, new_id)

💡 We changed the ground but didn't provide additional details for the view or the forest: the model will generally preserve most of the trees.

Now that the valley-forest sequence is over, we can journey up to the mountains, using the original mountain scene as our reference to return to that environment:

source_ids = [AssetId.ROBOT, AssetId.MOUNTAINS]
prompt = """
- Image 1: Reference robot character sheet.
- Image 2: Previous scene.
- Scene: A medium-wide shot of the robot climbing a broad, dome-shaped, medium-green mountain.
- Composition: The mountain is centered, with the robot on the left slope shown from a 3/4 rear angle.
- Action & Details: The robot has both feet on the mountain and uses two miniature ice picks (felt, with brown handles and gray heads) to reach the summit, planting them into the bottom part of the white felt snowcap.
- Background: The distant mountain range spans the entire horizon.
"""
new_id = AssetId.ASCENSION

generate_image(source_ids, prompt, new_id)

💡 The mountain close-up, inferred from the blurred background, is pretty impressive.

Let's climb to the summit:

source_ids = [AssetId.ROBOT, AssetId.ASCENSION]
prompt = """
- Image 1: Reference robot character sheet.
- Image 2: Previous scene.
- The robot reaches the top and stands on the summit, seen from the front.
- It is no longer holding the ice picks, which are planted upright in the snow on either side.
- It has both arms raised as a sign of victory. Its face and hands are unchanged.
"""
new_id = AssetId.SUMMIT

generate_image(source_ids, prompt, new_id)

💡 This is a logical follow-up but also a great alternative view.

Now, let's try something different to significantly recompose the scene:

source_ids = [AssetId.ROBOT, AssetId.SUMMIT]
prompt = """
- Image 1: Reference robot character sheet.
- Image 2: Previous scene.
- Remove the ice picks.
- Move the center mountain to the left edge of the image and add a slightly taller medium-blue mountain to the right edge.
- Suspend a stylized felt bridge between the two mountains: its deck is made of stylized thick planks of plain felt in various wood shades.
- Place the robot in the center of the bridge with one arm pointing toward the blue mountain.
- Maintain the background.
- View: Close-up.
"""
new_id = AssetId.BRIDGE

generate_image(source_ids, prompt, new_id)
  • This imperative prompt composes the scene in terms of actions. It's sometimes easier than writing descriptions.
  • A new mountain is added as instructed, and it is both different and consistent.
  • The bridge attaches to the summits in a very plausible way and seems to obey the laws of physics.
  • The "Remove the ice picks" instruction is there for a reason. Without it, the model would need to decide what to do with them (leave them planted, have the robot carry them, or something else entirely), leading to random results.
  • It's also possible to get the robot to walk on the bridge, seen from the side (which we haven't generated before), but getting it to consistently walk from left to right is tricky. Adding left and right views to the character sheet should fix this.

Let's generate a final scene and let the robot get some well-deserved rest:

source_ids = [AssetId.ROBOT, AssetId.BRIDGE]
prompt = """
- Image 1: Reference robot character sheet.
- Image 2: Previous scene.
- The robot is sleeping peacefully in a comfortable brown-and-tan tartan hammock that has replaced the bridge.
- Both of the robot's eyes are closed, in a "sleeping" state.
"""
new_id = AssetId.HAMMOCK

generate_image(source_ids, prompt, new_id)

💡 What's interesting here:

  • This time, the prompt is descriptive, and it works just as well as the previous imperative one.
  • The bridge-hammock transformation is really nice and preserves the attachments on the mountain summits.
  • The robot's transformation is also impressive, as it hasn't been seen in this position before, nor with closed eyes.

We've illustrated our story with nine new, consistent images! Let's take a step back to understand what we've built…

We now have a collection of image assets, from the original archive to brand-new images.

Let's add some data visualization to get a better sense of the steps completed…

Our new assets are all related, connected by one or more "generated from" links. In terms of data structures, this is a directed graph.

We can build the corresponding directed graph using the  library:

import networkx as nx


def build_graph(assets: Assets) -> nx.DiGraph:
    graph = nx.DiGraph(assets=assets)
    # Nodes
    for asset in assets.values():
        graph.add_node(asset.id, asset=asset)
    # Edges
    for asset in assets.values():
        for source_id in asset.source_ids:
            graph.add_edge(source_id, asset.id)
    return graph


asset_graph = build_graph(assets)
print(asset_graph)

DiGraph with 10 nodes and 16 edges

Let's place the most-used asset in the center and display the other assets around it:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def display_basic_graph(graph: nx.Graph) -> None:
    pos = compute_node_positions(graph)
    color = "#4285F4"
    nx.draw(
        graph,
        pos,
        with_labels=True,
        node_color=color,
        edge_color=color,
        arrowstyle="wedge",
        font_size="small",
        bbox=dict(ec="black", fc="white", alpha=0.7),
    )
    plt.show()


def compute_node_positions(graph: nx.Graph) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    if not graph.nodes:
        return {}
    # Put the most connected node in the center
    center_node = most_connected_node(graph)
    edge_nodes = set(graph) - {center_node}
    pos = nx.circular_layout(graph.subgraph(edge_nodes))
    pos[center_node] = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
    return pos


def most_connected_node(graph: nx.Graph) -> str:
    if not graph.nodes:
        return ""
    return max(graph.nodes, key=graph.degree)


display_basic_graph(asset_graph)

That's an accurate summary of our generation steps. It would be nice if we could also visualize our assets…

Let's add custom  functions to render the graph nodes with the assets in a more visually appealing way:

import typing
from collections.abc import Iterator
from pathlib import Path

import PIL.Image
import PIL.ImageDraw
from google.genai.types import PIL_Image
from matplotlib.axes import Axes
from matplotlib.backends.backend_agg import FigureCanvasAgg
from matplotlib.figure import Figure
from matplotlib.image import AxesImage
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from matplotlib.text import Annotation
from matplotlib.transforms import Bbox, TransformedBbox


@enum.unique
class ImageFormat(enum.StrEnum):
    # Matches PIL.Image.Image.format
    WEBP = enum.auto()
    PNG = enum.auto()
    GIF = enum.auto()


def yield_generation_graph_frames(
    graph: nx.DiGraph,
    animated: bool,
) -> Iterator[PIL_Image]:
    def get_fig_ax() -> tuple[Figure, Axes]:
        factor = 1.0
        figsize = (16 * factor, 9 * factor)
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
        fig.tight_layout(pad=3)
        handles = [
            Patch(color=COL_OLD, label="Archive"),
            Patch(color=COL_NEW, label="Generated"),
        ]
        ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower right")
        ax.set_axis_off()
        return fig, ax

    def prepare_graph() -> None:
        arrows = nx.draw_networkx_edges(graph, pos, ax=ax)
        if isinstance(arrows, list):
            for arrow in arrows:
                arrow.set_visible(False)

    def get_box_size() -> tuple[float, float]:
        xlim_l, xlim_r = ax.get_xlim()
        ylim_t, ylim_b = ax.get_ylim()
        factor = 0.08
        box_w = (xlim_r - xlim_l) * factor
        box_h = (ylim_b - ylim_t) * factor
        return box_w, box_h

    def add_axes() -> Axes:
        xf, yf = tr_figure(pos[node])
        xa, ya = tr_axes([xf, yf])
        x_y_w_h = (xa - box_w / 2.0, ya - box_h / 2.0, box_w, box_h)
        a = fig.add_axes(x_y_w_h)
        a.set_title(
            asset.id,
            loc="center",
            backgroundcolor="#FFF8",
            fontfamily="monospace",
            fontsize="small",
        )
        a.set_axis_off()
        return a

    def draw_box(color: str, image: bool) -> AxesImage:
        if image:
            result = pil_image.copy()
        else:
            result = PIL.Image.new("RGB", image_size, color="white")
        xy = ((0, 0), image_size)
        # Draw box outline
        draw = PIL.ImageDraw.Draw(result)
        draw.rounded_rectangle(xy, box_r, outline=color, width=outline_w)
        # Make everything outside the box outline transparent
        mask = PIL.Image.new("L", image_size, 0)
        draw = PIL.ImageDraw.Draw(mask)
        draw.rounded_rectangle(xy, box_r, fill=0xFF)
        result.putalpha(mask)
        return a.imshow(result)

    def draw_prompt() -> Annotation:
        text = f"Prompt:\n{asset.prompt}"
        margin = 2 * outline_w
        image_w, image_h = image_size
        bbox = Bbox([[0, margin], [image_w - margin, image_h - margin]])
        clip_box = TransformedBbox(bbox, a.transData)
        return a.annotate(
            text,
            xy=(0, 0),
            xytext=(0.06, 0.5),
            xycoords="axes fraction",
            textcoords="axes fraction",
            verticalalignment="center",
            fontfamily="monospace",
            fontsize="small",
            linespacing=1.3,
            annotation_clip=True,
            clip_box=clip_box,
        )

    def draw_edges() -> None:
        STYLE_STRAIGHT = "arc3"
        STYLE_CURVED = "arc3,rad=0.15"
        for parent in graph.predecessors(node):
            edge = (parent, node)
            color = COL_NEW if assets[parent].prompt else COL_OLD
            style = STYLE_STRAIGHT if center_node in edge else STYLE_CURVED
            nx.draw_networkx_edges(
                graph,
                pos,
                [edge],
                width=2,
                edge_color=color,
                style="dotted",
                ax=ax,
                connectionstyle=style,
            )

    def get_frame() -> PIL_Image:
        canvas = FigureCanvasAgg(fig)
        canvas.draw()
        image_bytes, image_size = canvas.print_to_buffer()
        return PIL.Image.frombytes("RGBA", image_size, image_bytes).convert("RGB")

    COL_OLD = "#34A853"
    COL_NEW = "#4285F4"
    assets = graph.graph["assets"]
    center_node = most_connected_node(graph)
    pos = compute_node_positions(graph)
    fig, ax = get_fig_ax()
    prepare_graph()
    box_w, box_h = get_box_size()
    tr_figure = ax.transData.transform  # Data → display coords
    tr_axes = fig.transFigure.inverted().transform  # Display → figure coords

    for node, data in graph.nodes(data=True):
        if animated:
            yield get_frame()
        # Edges and sub-plot
        asset = data["asset"]
        pil_image = asset.pil_image
        image_size = pil_image.size
        box_r = min(image_size) * 25 / 100  # Radius for rounded rect
        outline_w = min(image_size) * 5 // 100
        draw_edges()
        a = add_axes()  # a is used in sub-functions
        # Prompt
        if animated and asset.prompt:
            box = draw_box(COL_NEW, image=False)
            prompt = draw_prompt()
            yield get_frame()
            box.set_visible(False)
            prompt.set_visible(False)
        # Generated image
        color = COL_NEW if asset.prompt else COL_OLD
        draw_box(color, image=True)

    plt.close(fig)
    yield get_frame()


def draw_generation_graph(
    graph: nx.DiGraph,
    format: ImageFormat,
) -> BytesIO:
    frames = list(yield_generation_graph_frames(graph, animated=False))
    assert len(frames) == 1
    frame = frames[0]

    params: dict[str, typing.Any] = dict()
    match format:
        case ImageFormat.WEBP:
            params.update(lossless=True)

    image_io = BytesIO()
    frame.save(image_io, format, **params)

    return image_io


def draw_generation_graph_animation(
    graph: nx.DiGraph,
    format: ImageFormat,
) -> BytesIO:
    frames = list(yield_generation_graph_frames(graph, animated=True))
    assert 1 <= len(frames)

    if format == ImageFormat.GIF:
        # Dither all frames with the same palette to optimize the animation
        # The animation is cumulative, so most colors are in the last frame
        method = PIL.Image.Quantize.MEDIANCUT
        palettized = frames[-1].quantize(method=method)
        frames = [frame.quantize(method=method, palette=palettized) for frame in frames]

    # The animation will be played in a loop: start cycling with the most complete frame
    first_frame = frames[-1]
    next_frames = frames[:-1]
    INTRO_DURATION = 3000
    FRAME_DURATION = 1000
    durations = [INTRO_DURATION] + [FRAME_DURATION] * len(next_frames)
    params: dict[str, typing.Any] = dict(
        save_all=True,
        append_images=next_frames,
        duration=durations,
        loop=0,
    )
    match format:
        case ImageFormat.GIF:
            params.update(optimize=False)
        case ImageFormat.WEBP:
            params.update(lossless=True)

    image_io = BytesIO()
    first_frame.save(image_io, format, **params)

    return image_io


def display_generation_graph(
    graph: nx.DiGraph,
    format: ImageFormat | None = None,
    animated: bool = False,
    save_image: bool = False,
) -> None:
    if format is None:
        format = ImageFormat.WEBP if running_in_colab_env() else ImageFormat.PNG
    if animated:
        image_io = draw_generation_graph_animation(graph, format)
    else:
        image_io = draw_generation_graph(graph, format)

    image_bytes = image_io.getvalue()
    IPython.display.display(IPython.display.Image(image_bytes))

    if save_image:
        stem = "graph_animated" if animated else "graph"
        Path(f"./{stem}.{format.value}").write_bytes(image_bytes)

We can now display our generation graph:

display_generation_graph(asset_graph)

Have you ever generated something nice without saving the exact context?

Our assets can be made self-sufficient by saving prompts and source asset IDs (ancestors) in the image metadata (e.g., in PNG chunks), allowing for full local storage and retrieval (without needing a database or worrying about lost prompts!).

Let's add save-and-load functions, which might come in handy:

from datetime import datetime

from PIL.PngImagePlugin import PngInfo


def save_assets(assets: Assets) -> Path:
    # Saves assets to a dated folder
    now_here = datetime.now().astimezone()
    folder = Path(".") / now_here.strftime("%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S")
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for asset in assets.values():
        save_asset(asset, folder)
    return folder


def save_asset(asset: Asset, folder: Path) -> None:
    image_path = folder / f"{asset.id}.png"
    if image_path.is_file():
        raise FileExistsError(f'Asset file "{image_path}" already exists.')
    metadata = PngInfo()
    metadata.add_text("source_ids", "\n".join(asset.source_ids))
    metadata.add_text("prompt", asset.prompt)
    asset.pil_image.save(image_path, pnginfo=metadata)


def load_assets(folder: Path) -> Assets:
    assets = Assets()
    for image_path in sorted(folder.glob("*.png")):
        assets.set_asset(load_asset(image_path))
    return assets


def load_asset(image_path: Path) -> Asset:
    asset_id = image_path.stem
    with PIL.Image.open(image_path) as img:
        img.load()
        image_info = img.info
        source_ids = image_info.get("source_ids", "")
        source_ids = source_ids.split("\n") if source_ids else []
        prompt = image_info.get("prompt", "")
        image = img.copy()
    return Asset(asset_id, source_ids, prompt, image)


def demonstrate_save_and_load(assets: Assets) -> None:
    # Save
    folder = save_assets(assets)
    # Load & use
    loaded_assets = load_assets(folder)
    graph = build_graph(loaded_assets)
    display_generation_graph(graph)


# demonstrate_save_and_load(assets)

We generated a full set of new, consistent images with Nano Banana, and we learned a few things along the way:

  • This proves once again that a picture is worth a thousand words: it's now a lot easier to generate new images from existing ones using simple instructions.
  • We can create or edit images purely through composition (letting us all become art directors).
  • We can use descriptive or imperative instructions.
  • The model's spatial understanding enables 3D manipulation.
  • We can add text to our outputs (character sheet) and also refer to text in our inputs (front/back views).
  • Consistency can be preserved across various levels: character, scene, texture, lighting, camera angle/type…
  • The generation process can still be iterative, but it feels 10 to 100 times faster to get results that exceed expectations.
  • It is now possible to breathe new life into our archives!
  • The process we followed is essentially a generation pipeline. It can be adapted for automation (e.g., changing a node regenerates its descendants) or for generating multiple variations in parallel (e.g., the same set of images could be generated for different aesthetics, audiences, or simulations).
  • For the sake of clarity and exploration, the prompts are intentionally simple. In a production environment, they could have a fixed structure with a standardized set of parameters.
  • We described the scenes as if they were shot in a photo studio. Virtually any other imaginable artistic style is possible (photorealistic, abstract, 2D…).

As a bonus, let's end with an animated version of our journey, where the generation graph also offers a glimpse of our instructions:

display_generation_graph(asset_graph, animated=True)

items.title: Automattic's Board Forces CEO Matt Mullenweg Into Leave of Absence
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Automattic's board has placed founder and CEO Matt Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence against his will, with CFO Mark Davies taking over as interim CEO. The reason for the move remains unclear, but it follows years of legal fights, layoffs, employee departures, and controversy surrounding Mullenweg's leadership. TechCrunch reports: Earlier Wednesday, Mullenweg posted in a Slack channel visible to all employees that the company's chief financial officer, Mark Davies, had "conspired" with other board members Ann Dunwoody, Toni Schneider, and Sue Decker to vote to put Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence.
 
The message read: "And the biggest news: I won't be able to make the [meeting] tomorrow. @Mark Davies has conspired with @Ann Dunwoody, @Toni, and @Sue Decker behind my back and they voted to put me on a paid leave of absence. I voted against that. Wishing Mark and all of you the very best. To clarify @Mark Davies was voted as interim CEO. I received the resolution 50 minutes before the meeting start, and requested repeatedly for time to have it reviewed by independent legal counsel, even a few hours, which was denied."
 
A Slack message to the open source WordPress.org community from the project's executive director, Mary Hubbard, also confirmed Mullenweg's change of status at the commercial company. However, Hubbard said that WordPress.org was not impacted. "Matt remains the leader of the WordPress project and I remain Executive Director of WordPress. Our teams, priorities, and work continue as planned," she wrote.
