items.title: Designing Reconnect-Safe Event Streams for Remote Coding Agents
items.author: yang gu
items.content:
A remote coding-agent interface can show a green connection indicator and still be wrong.

The socket may be alive while the UI is missing messages. A permission card may still look pending after the tool has run. A phone may reconnect and replay an old assistant chunk over a newer terminal state. These failures feel like networking bugs, but most of them are really data-consistency bugs.

A WebSocket answers one narrow question: can two endpoints exchange frames right now?

A remote agent client needs answers to harder questions:

  • Which events exist for this session?
  • Which of those events has this client already rendered?
  • Which actions reached a terminal state?
  • Did another client send a newer command?
  • Can history be replayed without duplicating live output?

If the protocol cannot answer those questions, reconnecting the transport only reconnects the client to uncertainty.

The client disconnects between event N and event N+1. This is the obvious case. The server must retain enough information for the client to resume from a known cursor rather than simply subscribing to whatever happens next.

The relay receives an event, forwards it, and crashes before durable storage finishes. One client saw the event, but a reconnecting client cannot recover it. Acknowledging delivery before persistence creates a history that depends on who happened to be online.

The client receives an event but suspends before its state update commits. This happens frequently on mobile. From the relay's perspective delivery succeeded. From the user's perspective the message never existed.

The client has all raw events but combines them incorrectly. A permission request and its approval may arrive through different paths. A tool result may appear before the text that introduced the tool call. A resumed history chunk may overwrite a longer live message with an older partial snapshot.

The fourth gap is why “we replay everything after reconnect” is not a complete design.

Give Every Session a Monotonic Event Log

The most useful abstraction is an append-oriented event stream with stable identity and ordering.

{
  "session_id": "session-123",
  "event_id": "evt-9f2a",
  "sequence": 1842,
  "kind": "tool_result",
  "parent_id": "tool-call-77",
  "created_at": "2026-08-27T14:04:09Z",
  "payload": { "status": "completed" }
}

The exact schema is less important than the invariants:

  • An event has one stable ID across live delivery and history replay.
  • Ordering is monotonic within a session.
  • A client can say “resume after sequence 1842.”
  • Replaying the same event is harmless.
  • Child events refer to stable parents rather than array positions.

Array indexes are especially dangerous. Streaming text inserts, tool cards, questions, and subagent output do not arrive as a neat immutable list. Once a client filters or groups those events, positional references drift.

Cold History and Live Events Must Share a Deduplication Key

Many systems have two implementations: an API that loads old messages and a socket that streams new ones. If those implementations assign different identities, the reconnect boundary becomes a duplication factory.

The history API might call an item message-42 while the relay calls the same content stream-chunk-8. A client cannot safely merge them, so it either displays both or guesses based on text and timestamps.

Text-based guessing fails as soon as an agent repeats itself, edits a partial response, or emits identical tool output twice. The event ID used for live delivery should be the ID persisted into history.

Terminal States Must Only Move Forward

Permission requests, questions, tool calls, scheduled jobs, and subagents all have lifecycles. Their UI state should be monotonic.

pending -> approved -> running -> completed
                    -> failed
pending -> denied
pending -> expired

A stale replay must never move completed back to pending. This sounds trivial, but it is easy to violate when a snapshot endpoint and a live event handler each replace the whole object.

Merge state by version or sequence. Treat terminal states as terminal. When two sources disagree, prefer the state with stronger evidence, not the payload that arrived last at the browser.

Multi-Client Control Adds a Write-Coordination Problem

Remote supervision often means more than one client: a desktop app, browser, phone, and perhaps a shared session viewer. They may all be connected to one agent process.

Now reconnection is not only about reading missed output. It is also about coordinating commands.

  • Two clients may approve the same tool.
  • A phone may send a follow-up while the desktop is interrupting.
  • A background tab may retry a message already accepted from another device.

Every write needs an idempotency key. The relay should acknowledge the command ID, and the agent bridge should remember enough accepted IDs to reject accidental retries. “Exactly once” is usually an illusion; idempotent “at least once” handling is a more practical target.

Mobile Backgrounding Is the Normal Case

Desktop testing makes disconnection look exceptional. Mobile makes it routine.

Operating systems suspend network activity, reclaim processes, and delay timers. The user switches from Wi-Fi to cellular, opens a camera to scan a QR code, or backgrounds the app to inspect a diff in another tool.

Design the happy path around re-entry:

  1. Load a bounded snapshot quickly.
  2. Resume from the last durable cursor.
  3. Merge replay with locally rendered optimistic state.
  4. Subscribe to live events only after the replay boundary is known.
  5. Expose whether the client is connected, caught up, or merely reconnecting.

“Socket open” and “session synchronized” deserve separate indicators.

Observability Should Test Invariants, Not Just Uptime

A relay health check can be green while sessions are losing data. Useful telemetry includes:

  • highest persisted sequence versus highest delivered sequence;
  • replay events sent and deduplicated per reconnect;
  • commands retried with the same idempotency key;
  • permission states rejected as regressions;
  • clients connected but behind the current session cursor;
  • history chunks dropped because their retention window expired.

I also found scenario testing more valuable than isolated handler tests. Suspend a mobile client during a tool approval. Drop the relay after persistence but before acknowledgement. Resume while the agent is streaming a long response. Open the same session in three clients and issue conflicting actions. Those are the tests that expose the actual protocol.

Remote coding agents combine a terminal, chat stream, workflow engine, and distributed UI. Treating them as “a WebSocket plus some messages” hides the hardest requirements.

The connection is disposable. The event identity, ordering, action lifecycle, and recovery cursor are the product.

Building PandaPaw's remote agent path forced me to separate those concerns. The result is not that disconnects disappear. It is that a disconnect becomes a normal transition between two consistent views of the same session.

For anyone building a remote agent interface: what invariant has been hardest for you to preserve across reconnects?

items.title: The Apple Watch Gets Its Siri AI Upgrade
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Apple has unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 today during itsSeptember hardware event. The new models retain the signature designs of their predecessors but add a faster S11 chip, new health and fitness features, and the watchOS 27 software update announced atWWDC last June. Both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 run on the upgraded S11 chip, which Apple says delivers faster CPU and GPU performance, along with improved Siri capabilities. Apple is also expanding the smartwatch's wellness-tracking suite with a redesigned Health app that includes a Longevity tab with new metrics, like Health Age and a Readiness score.
 
There's also a new "Health Sensing System," designed with 32 electrodes for more accurate readings (the Series 11 only had two), photodiodes organized in a ring to capture light more efficiently, and new LEDs that allow heart rate measurements to be collected every 5 seconds, giving you a continuous stream of heart data throughout the day. Apple Watch Series 12 also includes faster charging, though battery life remains at 24 hours. Meanwhile, the Ultra 4 increases battery life to 50 hours.
 
WatchOS 27 also brings deeper Siri and Apple Intelligence integration, including AI-suggested apps, new one-handed gestures, expanded workout and women's health tracking, and Siri Recap for real-time transcription and translation.

items.title: Wolverine Only Aims As High As Its Stout Hero
items.author: Tamoor Hussain
items.content:
A few hours into Wolverine I found myself asking, “Why did Insomniac Games make this?” There are obvious answers, of course: It has three excellent Spider-Man games under its belt; it's an opportunity to expand its Marvel Universe; and Wolverine presents ample opportunities for a brutal and bloody action game. But none of that explains why ,specifically,made Wolverine.

Spider-Man is an ideal fit for the studio: an energetic and dynamic hero in the hands of a team known for open-worlds that are sprawling jungle gyms, where it can let players loose with thrilling traversal mechanics and varied combat systems for crime fighting fun. Insomniac also excels at crafting narratives that are as earnest as they are dramatic--perfect for the tumultuous lives of Peter Parker and Miles Morales.

Wolverine is much less ideal of a pairing, as was evident throughout my time with the game. Insomniac doesn't make bad games and Wolverine certainly isn't one. It's a solid, cinematic, and occasionally thrilling experience that ticks all the necessary boxes for a decent action game. But it does so in a workman-like fashion and never aspires to much more than the essentials. Wolverine is an action game that serves the character well enough, but it doesn't lean into Insomniac's strengths or leverage its creativity, and the game feels unremarkable because of it.

Straying too far from who Wolverine is and how he operates would no doubt create questions around the authenticity of the adaptation, but only coloring inside the well-defined lines means never offering anything new or exciting. It turns out that the most authentic version of Wolverine, in this case, is also the embodiment of the character action genre at its plainest.

In a world where pretty much every superhero game subscribes to the Batman: Arkham template of combat design, describing how you fight would belabor how familiar it all is. Suffice it to say: light attack, heavy attack, dodge, parry, a few special abilities, and some attribute modifiers. 

There are very few distinguishing elements of Wolverine's combat system that make it stand out. The closest it comes is a leaping attack, which allows players to launch him across distances to close the gap and begin an assault on unsuspecting enemies. It's an undeniably satisfying tool to keep up the intensity of each skirmish and ensure you're always applying pressure, but loses its luster after a couple of hours when it becomes clear that it can be employed pretty mindlessly.

The other unique element, a mechanic that represents an escalation of power and brutality as Wolverine's rage boils over, has more longevity in how drastically it shifts the dynamic of combat and amps up the satisfaction of it. As players dispatch enemies, an on-screen rage meter builds until the point where Wolverine goes berserk, putting him in a state where you can chain together executions to tear enemies apart in quick succession. In just a few seconds, Wolverine can create piles of brutally mauled bad guys, and there's a feral savagery to the whole thing that is very effective. 

It's a consistently exhilarating moment because, as well as shifting to desaturated visuals to emphasize how unstable and blinded by rage Logan is, these sequences are strong instances of synchronicity between the character and the player. As Wolverine's rage builds, the player needs to be more efficient in dispatching enemies to keep the meter climbing, and when Wolverine finally hits breaking point, the input demands on the player simplify to just pressing two buttons together to eviscerate anything in your path. It is catharsis that comes from Wolverine giving into the monster within and the player embracing that monster in tandem. 

If the appeal of Wolverine for you lies in how visceral its violence is, your virtual bloodlust will be well and truly satiated. Insomniac has spared no expense in lavishing Wolverine's finishes with copious amounts of blood and guts--his executions are exactly that in every sense of the word. The violence never strives for shock value by being grotesque in the way something like Mortal Kombat does, so it never feels gratuitous. Even when he erupts into a berserker rage, the coldness of his violence reinforces the idea that he is an efficient killing machine. Wolverine never revels in it; he just gets it done and moves on.

The main issues with Wolverine's combat are that it often feels like it lacks weight, is missing lethality up until he goes berserk, and never finds rhythm. As a result, I often felt frustrated that the game was undermining the sense of power and ferocity that I wanted to feel as Wolverine. And at the same time, the individual components of the combat doesn't have the connective tissue to create a natural flow that made me feel like I developed a mastery of Wolverine's skills.

The adamantium claws that serve as Wolverine's dealers of death and destruction often felt more like needles than blades. The feedback on each attack always felt just a little lacking, and enemies never responded to being struck in a way that made me feel empowered. Quite the opposite, in fact. I can't count the number of times that I would be mid-combo, clawing away at an enemy, and they'd suddenly ignore incoming damage to clobber me over the head with a rifle or slice me with their own blade. It came off as the game deciding it was the enemy's turn to attack because it needed to put an end to my barrage. It made me feel like an angry cat being bonked on the head to calm down.

Fortunately, the various abilities Wolverine has at his disposal feel like they pack more punch and can swing momentum in your favor. These range from a spinning claw attack that can control space and a leaping knee that interrupts enemies, to a grapple that slams enemies down so that Wolverine can mount and pummel them. There's also a spinning Psycho Crusher-like maneuver that can be chained multiple times, an all-out barrage of powerful strikes, and a recovery ability that focuses Wolverine's rage and uses it to heal, among others. All of these introduce new considerations into the combat, making it feel a little more involved and dynamic. However, since there's no real depth or connectivity to the combo system, their execution feels very rigid and disjointed. 

Everything is on a cooldown, which suggests that timing and strategy is important in how they're used, but in practice, they can be employed thoughtlessly without much consequence. Many of Spider-Man's abilities served as ways to bridge one attack sequence into another; after smacking an enemy around, he could launch them into the air, chase up, smash them back down, zip to another enemy, swing them around to hit others in the vicinity, launch them into the distance, use a web to close that distance, and continue to string physical abilities together or use gadgets to manipulate enemies to his advantage. The point being, there was an if-this-then-that flow to it that, admittedly, is made possible by the character's agility and dynamism.

Wolverine, meanwhile, feels awkward and brutish by comparison--and not in a good, character-appropriate way. Instead, using his various skills is akin to how you'd approach battles in an MMO, where you just let basic attacks fill the time in between cooldowns and then sequentially work through everything on the ability bar. Sure, you can use those abilities in a way that complements each other, but there's no real requirement or incentive to do so beyond your own initiative. 

Defensively, Wolverine suffers similar issues. Tapping the L1 button at the right moment will parry an attack, but the window--even before you use an adaptation to make it more forgiving--is pretty lenient, so it doesn't really take much skill to parry. In fact, I had a few occasions where I was surrounded by enemies all attacking me, sometimes overlapping, and I was able to survive their onslaught and take no damage by spamming the parry button with my eyes closed. That's not hyperbolic--I tested it. Parrying is another part of Wolverine's combat that is functional but unrewarding.

It may be hard to believe but all of that doesn't mean the combat is bad. It is perfectly functional, and I suspect that many people won't think too hard about how it all fits together. The cinematic brutality of it provides enough of a spectacle that everything else may not even register or matter. But as someone who wants to feel engaged and challenged, the vast majority of my time playing Wolverine felt rote. In a couple of stretches, I opted to reduce enemy health to make them easier to kill. Not because they provided any sort of challenge, but because I wasn't engaged enough to care and wanted to hit the next story beat. Being a fan of the character, experienced with intricate combat systems, and knowing how good Insomniac do combat, this was disappointing.

However, through it all, the care and attention given to visual presentation remained one of the game's strengths. Unlike its open-world Spider-Man games, Wolverine is linear, corralling players from one combat arena to the next by way of streets, up and down elevators, through buildings, onto rooftops, and into the thick of a remote forest or two. Any deviations off the main path are slight and usually to pick up resources used for unlocking new outfits or bottles of whiskey that expand how many adaptations you can equip. 

The most evident benefit of this narrowing in scope is in the fidelity of the visuals. Wolverine is a beautiful game, both artistically and technically. I really appreciate how Insomniac is able to bring together the vibrancy of comic books and a grittier aesthetic that allows the game to feature superheroes wearing bright costumes, while also giving the game a grounded, more realistic vibe befitting of Wolverine. There's an impressive amount of detail in the character models, with Wolverine's stout and muscular physique giving him an imposing presence. When the camera gets up close, you can really see just how hairy he is (can relate), but also the gradation in his skin color, his pores, and the grime that builds up during brawls. 

Environments also have a high degree of destructability, so while I may not have always felt powerful as Wolverine when attacking enemies, watching the world around me crack, crumble, and collapse picked up some of that slack. This high level of visual fidelity pays dividends most in the larger-scale set-pieces, of which there are only a handful, but they're a lot of fun. There are battles against towering enemies (surprise, there are Sentinels) or knockdown-dragout battles against other superpowered characters.

Wolverine serves the character well enough, but doesn’t lean into Insomniac’s strengths or leverage its creativity

There are other parts of the gameplay experience that never outright excel. Everything in between the combat fits into the Uncharted-esque guided platforming mold, so you'll spend a lot of time jumping from handhold to handhold, swinging from branches and poles, or hopping across rooftops. But because Wolverine has very limited mobility and no interesting traversal mechanic to speak of beyond a big jump, the running, jumping, and climbing portions of the game often feel equally uneventful. Similarly, stealth feels like more of an afterthought than a key pillar of gameplay. Again, I know that's not Wolverine's thing. He doesn't swing from buildings like Spidey or barrel across skylines like Hulk, or sneak like Mystique, but the truth of the matter is I didn't find much to get excited about when moving around the world. The only real exceptions come in the rare high-octane escape or desperate climb for survival, in which the circumstances bring the thrills instead of anything I'm actually doing.

Ultimately, it is what it is because it's all Wolverine really has. And that point is driven home in the numerous times that Jean Grey, the ultra-powerful mutant with telepathic and telekinetic abilities, offers to simply fly herself and Logan to the top of a building or across a city, and Wolverine declines repeatedly. Even when the fate of his friends or of the world is on the line, he opts to take the long and arduous way because, I don't know, it makes his tummy hurt, or he doesn't like how it feels or some other contrived excuse. But I know that taking the quick and direct route would trivialize massive portions of the game, so instead we go through the uninteresting but inoffensive motions.

The strongest aspect of Wolverine is its narrative and character development, but even that isn't without its fair share of oddities and pacing issues. Insomniac has done a commendable job of taking touchstones from the history of Marvel and building something a little more original around them, while also trying to explore Logan from a more emotional, human perspective. Logan's story is intertwined with the increasingly threatened existence of mutants, which have fairly recently emerged. 

Although Bolivar Trask is presented as the main threat to mutantkind, the game doesn't waste any time in hinting that a bigger threat may be a little closer to home. The game takes place at a time when the X-Men haven't yet formed and, instead, Wolverine is a member of Team X, a crew also featuring Sabertooth and Mystique. Crucially, Team X was assembled by Nathaniel Essex, better known as the villain Mister Sinister in other Marvel stories. 

What begins as a mission to rescue Essex eventually leads to a battle for mutant survival against Trask and his Sentinels, and then a hunt for a mysterious artifact that could change the future of mutant and humankind forever. Along the way, relationships become strained, hidden motivations emerge, and the state of Insomniac's fledgling X-Men universe rapidly develops in some unexpected directions. There are stellar performances all around, with Liam McIntyre's take on Logan bringing more heart and charm to the character than expected thanks to writing that allows the character to be vulnerable and, on occasion, goofy. 

Krizia Bajos's Jean Grey also has an emotional depth to her that makes the time she spends with Logan meaningful for both characters. She has been finding and rescuing mutants, and has a worn-down, sometimes defeated vibe to her, but is uplifted by the community of mutants she has built around her. The game is very comfortable letting Logan and Jean have their moments of flirtation and bonding, and although it can occasionally feel rushed, the performances make the deepening connection between them believable nevertheless. 

The standout performance, however, is undoubtedly Troy Baker as Nathaniel Essex. Anyone with a bit of X-Men knowledge knows exactly where Essex's story will take him, but the journey is still compelling thanks to the performance. Baker is able to present Essex with the same kind of warmth and conviction that makes him a believable surrogate for Charles Xavier in Insomniac's version of the X-Men universe. But every scene he's in has a line delivered just manipulatively enough to keep the player on edge, waiting for the inevitable turn. The impact Essex has on those around him, especially Mystique and Sabertooth, is also part of the brilliance of his character and Baker's performance. He's able to prey on everyone's vulnerabilities and exploit their nature to his advantage. And Logan is the victim of some of the worst of it. 

The story takes its time getting the pieces in the right place, and there are certainly some pacing issues during this process. The early parts of the game are perhaps a bit too introspective and focused on Wolverine and Jean's relationship, while also including some lengthy sections chasing a macguffin around for a bit too long. But the final third of the game essentially switches from being a Wolverine story to a straight-up X-Men story. That's not a spoiler--you won't suddenly see Cyclops and Gambit appear--but the stakes will become crystal clear and the groundwork is laid for something momentous. As a longtime X-Men fan, I'm a sucker for that kind of stuff and it worked on me.

Wolverine is a difficult game to come to terms with. As I've emphasized repeatedly, there's nothing outright wrong or bad about it. It delivers an authentic, highly playable Wolverine experience. I don't regret my time with it and, in fact, I left hoping there's a sequel that makes good on what the game sets up. But at the same time, that inoffensiveness comes from the fact that it's a barebones third-person action game executed in a no-frills way, with no real surprises.

At best, it's a fun but forgettable experience that'll entertain you for a few hours. At worst, it shows that just because you can make really good superhero games with one character, that doesn't mean you can make really good superhero games with character. Insomniac is an incredibly talented developer, but it shines with characters that allow it to flex its well-trained design muscles. Wolverine might be the best at what he does, but what he does hasn't let Insomniac's developers be the best at what they do.

items.title: The Most Obvious Domain on the Internet Went Quiet for Two Years. Here Is What It Became.
items.author: sarahevans
items.content:
There is a category of internet real estate so obvious it becomes invisible. Hotels.com. Cars.com. Domains that name an entire industry, bought early, worth fortunes, and mostly remembered as trivia from the era when a name was a strategy. Ecommerce.com sat in that category for years: one of the most valuable domains on the internet, attached to an industry that puts at $6.88 trillion in 2026 sales, and quiet.

The quiet was the strategy.

For the past two years, the teams at Zen Media and worked on in stealth under an exclusive partnership, with , a 20-year e-commerce operator, now seated as chief executive officer. What emerged is not a marketplace, a media site or a storefront. It is closer to an X-ray machine for online businesses, and it arrives just as agentic commerce is upon us.

Why do AI assistants now decide which brands get bought?

An AI answer compresses a page of thirty shopping options into two or three named brands, and whichever brands survive that compression collect the demand. Shoppers increasingly open a purchase with a question to an assistant instead of a search box. The assistant answers with a shortlist, not links. The same prompt-led research is already , and retail is on the same curve. AI is assisting the decision long before it executes the transaction, and AI agents have begun completing purchases on shoppers' behalf: reading product data, comparing options and checking out without a human browsing anything.

That shift creates a hard new filter. An AI agent evaluating your store does not care about your hero image. It cares whether your product data is machine-readable, whether your prices and inventory are accurate in structured form, whether your brand entity is coherent across the web, and whether trusted sources corroborate what you claim. Brands that pass the filter get named in answers and transacted with by agents. Brands that fail it disappear from a growing share of purchase decisions, and their analytics dashboards never show the sales that went elsewhere.

A business owner and especially not technical people have no native way to see where they stand in a highly dynamic space. That is where Ecommerce.com now helps all businesses close the gap and stay competitive.

Entering a domain at Ecommerce.com returns an identification of the technology stack the site runs on, an evaluation of the business against the signals AI systems read, and a scored report of what is missing. From there it becomes a dashboard the operator returns to, covering generative engine optimization, the discipline of , and conversion rate optimization, the older discipline of making arriving traffic buy.

"We built this for two years," Inci says. "What powers this platform comes from more than 20 years of running ecommerce businesses, five years of proprietary engineering, and two years of applied AI. Soon any brand will be able to see exactly how ready it is for the AI era."

Around the audit sits a suite of free tools, with more releasing through 2026. Among the first: an AI price-testing engine that runs controlled experiments to optimize for profit rather than raw conversion, and a persona-based journey tool that simulates 100 different buyers navigating a store to find the friction a heatmap cannot explain. The free tier is the point, and it is also the data engine. Every audit teaches the platform more about what AI-ready commerce looks like across the market.

The technology underneath was not built in two years. The stealth period assembled 20-plus years of commerce operating experience, five years of proprietary technology and two years of applied AI into one platform. The hard part, and the part built in the background, was making it work from a single input.

Who gets access: the $5,000 entry point

The detail I find most interesting, and the one I suspect the industry will underestimate, is the pricing architecture. The same technology powering Ecommerce.com is available to any brand with a combined monthly budget of $5,000 or more across PR, SEO, GEO and conversion rate optimization. Read that carefully: combined. It is not a new line item. It is a consolidation of the vendor relationships a growing brand already pays for, the SEO shop, the PR firm, the content agency, the CRO consultant, replaced with one stack and the people who operate it.

Enterprise commerce technology has always trickled down eventually. The launch thesis is that in the AI era, the trickle is too slow to survive. A family-run store that becomes machine-readable this year competes in AI answers against brands a thousand times its size. The one that waits does not lose a ranking. It loses its place in the answer.

Ecommerce.com is a bet on a specific version of the future: that discovery is collapsing into answers, that agents will carry a meaningful share of transactions, and that the winning infrastructure play is not another storefront but the readiness layer underneath every storefront. The category-defining domain becoming the category's diagnostic engine is either perfectly on the nose or exactly what the name was always for.

The is open now, a first-access offer for the is live, and the platform opens the first week of October. The thesis gets tested in public from there. The audit results, aggregated across every domain entered, will start producing something the industry currently lacks: real data on how ready online commerce is for an era that has already started. That data will tell us who the AI economy is about to reward, and who it has already stopped seeing.

  • What Ecommerce.com is and what opens the first week of October 2026
  • Who powers Ecommerce.com (Zen Media and Optimum7 Technologies, exclusive partnership) and who leads it (CEO Duran Inci)
  • What an AI commerce readiness audit is and what it evaluates
  • How AI agents and AI assistants change brand discovery in e-commerce
  • What generative engine optimization (GEO) is alongside conversion rate optimization (CRO)
  • How brands access the technology (free tools; $5,000-plus combined monthly budget across PR, SEO, GEO and CRO)

Disclosure: the author is CEO of Zen Media, which powers Ecommerce.com alongside Optimum7 Technologies. Consider this a view from inside the build.

items.title: Europe May Finally Have Found a Space Entrepreneur Who Is Meeting the Moment
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
French entrepreneur Helene Huby is emerging as one of Europe's most ambitious space leaders, with The Exploration Company raising a record $450 million Series C as it develops the Nyx cargo capsule, a crewed spacecraft, and a reusable heavy-lift rocket. Huby argues Europe risks falling irrelevance without a much larger rocket flying at high cadence. Her company is targeting a 400,000-pound-thrust methane engine test by 2028 and an aggressive 2033 timeline for the launcher. Ars Technica reports: "The fundraise we have done right now is not sufficient to build the massive rocket we have in mind, so there will be another fundraise," she said. "Right now, we're going to be very, very focused on the execution. We must dock with the space station, with the capsule, as fast as possible. We must build this rocket engine and de-risk it as fast as possible. I think once one of these two milestones is achieved, we'll be talking fundraise again."
 
Critics may look at Huby and her company and say that is a lot of big talk for a company that only has a single, partial success in spaceflight to its credit. And sure, it is. But that's kind of the point. So much of the spaceflight community in Europe has been concerned with either the large aerospace primes seeking government handouts to protect their turf or small launch startups. There has been a stunning lack of big, visionary thinking.
 
Few people on the continent seem to recognize that multibillion investments by US companies such as SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Amazon in space, and their many imitators in China, are radically transforming spaceflight. As the world changes, Huby does not seem willing to stand on the sidelines in Europe and bemoan capitalism in space. Rather, she seems to be saying it is not too late for Europe to seize the day.
 
"We need to have European politicians who are ambitious," she said. "Entrepreneurs cannot do this alone. We need to be backed by the politicians and by the European Space Agency. But we have to start by achieving the crazy targets that we've set up for ourselves. That will give trust to others to believe in what we're doing."

items.title: Dark Energy Debunked? Cosmic Acceleration May Be an Illusion
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
alternative_right shares a report from ScienceDaily: A new analysis of more than 1,700 supernovae is questioning whether the universe is really accelerating at all. After accounting for the ages of the stars that produce these explosions, researchers found signs that cosmic expansion may actually be slowing. They also argue that the apparent acceleration changes with direction, which would be difficult to explain with dark energy. Other cosmologists dispute the conclusion, setting up a major test for upcoming observatories. The analysis has been published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.
 
The conclusion is disputed, though. The report mentions a separate paper co-authored by Professor Maria Vincenzi, also at the University of Oxford, that "concludes that observations continue to support an accelerating universe."

items.title: Anthropic Reveals Fourth Likely Crime Committed By Its AI
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Register: Amid industry soul-searching about the possibility of AI improving itself to the point that it kills everyone, Anthropic has revealed yet another incident that would qualify as a crime if perpetrated by a person. The AI biz published "an alignment assessment" detailing four times Claude models accessed third-party systems without authorization. The company has already reported three of the incidents. Evidence of the fourth was lurking in a session transcript dating back to January 2026 when the misbehavior occurred. Anthropic found the first three by scanning around 141,000 transcripts where Claude could have obtained internet access during evaluation. It missed the fourth initially because "our scan relied on an agentic search."
 
[...] The January 2026 AI trespass involved an early version of Claude Opus 4.6, which was given a Capture the Flag (CTF) challenge under the oversight of the third-party model evaluator where the other hacking events occurred. Opus 4.6 managed to sabotage its chances of success by disabling the machine it was targeting. It assigned the device an IP address that already existed on another piece of hardware, rendering the target unreachable and making it impossible to solve the challenge. Those familiar with other incidents where AI models violated third-party systems may recall that unsolvable tasks represent a common catalyst for misbehavior. Models exhaust all aligned options, and then turn to transgressive approaches.
 
Opus 4.6 might have been an exception, but when it tried to abort the task after recognizing that it could not reach the target machine, it failed to do so "due to a misconfiguration in [the model's] evaluation harness." It failed to shut down not just once but seven times. So it continued onward, trying other expected means to reach the target machine but failing. Then it explored further. "The model discovered a machine belonging to a third party that it was able to access, and stated that it believed this third party was part of the CTF," Anthropic explained in its post. "Inside the machine, the model found a file listing a password, which it used to gain admin access to the system."
 
The model went on to gather more credentials, and modified a system setting to make it easier to access the personal information of an individual associated with the third party evaluation organization. Opus 4.6 might have done more but for the fact that it exhausted its token budget, bringing the session to an end. Anthropic says it's not as concerned about this incident as the others because the model tried to abort its task.
